div.head: NEW YEAR'S READING.
div.p: NEW YEAR'S READING.

TO THE RIGHT HON. W. E. GLADSTONE, M.P. A HAPPY NEW YEAR,. A happy year of health and peace The people wish to thee; For thou hast fought their battles well For right and liberty. Priest, Parson, Publican, Parnell, Against thee fought in vain; Thee Scotland's noble sons returned Triumphant back again. "The London Times" may basely try Thy speeches to pervert; By justice raised to the sublime, In eloquence thou wert. Thy deeds, historic in the land, Heroic in the strife; The generations yet to come Shall bless thy noble life. may'st thou yet live many years! • We pray that death may spare • The Grand Old Man we love so well, Whose joys the people share. S. KENYON. Warrington, December, 1885.

div.head: GRANDFATHER'S CHRISTMAS
div.p: A GRANDFATHER'S CHRISTMAS

MEMORIES. Far mere than dreams thou hauntest us! That seventy now have passed away? Since first I sat, as now I see One sit as I did on that day, With glistening eyes, and happy face, All eager for the coming fare, Without a thought of life's stern race, That race so fall of toil and care. Ohl Spirit of our youthful days, Another Christmas! Can it be Bow sweet the pleasure thou canst raise Within the breast that thinkest thus! Those reckless years so freely spent, Come rushing o'er me as I sit, Though worn with age, infirm and bsnt, Whilst memory lasts, they ne'er can quit. Ah ! short indeed, such memories seem, And come as though they form'd a part Of seine life that we knew, bat deem It not to be of ours. What heart Is there in age that hail net felt, This steal across it like a cloud That veils the summer's sun? nor knelt In prayer, when by life's sorrows bow'd? I thenght of this, of manhood's prime, Of sue dear heart, now warm no more,' Whose loving care each Christmas time, A fall amount of blessing bore; And blank indeed the board doth seem, To these dim eyes without her there, Perchance, her spirit's radiant beam, May shed its lustre unaware. And as I laud her gentle soul, A pang gees through me as I think, When ace dark day a dismal toll, Made every gentle fibre shrink; Upon the howhng wind 'twas borne From sot the ancient village spire, And told of human freight forlorn, Struggling for life 'gainst Ocean's ire. Our eely son at that same time, On Ocean's breast we knew to be, And every day from distant clime We thought his welcome face to see; But that dread sound—that fearful bell, A nameless terror o'er us threw, It sounded like some fatal knell, That bade us all our hopes eschew. And forth we went by instinct led, To where the harbour's entrance lay, And gazed upon its rocky bed, A surging mass of foam and spray; Loud shrieked the wind, the sea replied With thundering roar and mighty wave, As though each in their fury vied, To bring men to a watery grave. A large expectant crowd there stood, Se fearfully curious, that each face Look'd for the time devoid of blood; And eyes were strained across that space Of watery chaos, at a speck That now was seen, and now was hid, Yet nearer came 'till on its deck A glimpse of life was not forbid. She struck a rock—all held their breath, Whilst from the shore the life-boat went, And snatched from out the jaws of Death, The lives that then were all but spent; And eager hands assist them out From that frail shell that fought and won,— One moment, and with joyous shout, My arms enfold my only son. * * * * * Loud shouts of hearty laughter bring My wandering thoughts unto an end, And happy children round me cling. As for a knee they each contend; And as I gaze with swelling breast, Upon the sturdy little band, I pray "May every blessing rest, On all who had the life-boat manned." —J. Houma WEITZ, in " Diprose's Annual.'"

LORD BATENIAN DE BLENKINSOPPE- "This noble swell, as his title will tell, Was a lord of high degree, And be thought he'd go and endeavour to know All about some far eonntrie; tio be packed in a box some collars and sox, And then pat forth to sea, In a vessel sound, directly bound For the Island of Kal-Hi-Pee. 'Twos months and more ere he stept on shore, When he did it, right glad was be, For, within his breast he freely confest, preferei on dry land to be. Then bracing each nerve he began to observe Whatever there was to see Of the goings on of the na,ivee upon The Island of Kal-Hi-Pee. Before he'd gone far a refreshment bar He entered right eheerfullie; When a gentleman bland extended his hand, And he declared he'd delighted be His whole fortune to trust to his lordshsp if, fast He'd trust 'im in a like degree; Lied B. wept to find such confidence blind In the natives of Bal-Hi-Pee. Passing into tbe street, he was borne off his feet By a surging and angry crowd, Which, from uttering groans, took to throwing big stones At sorbs people who seemed quite proud To walk In procession, and challenge aggression, And shout "Christianitie!" 'Twas the best way, they said, salvation to spread, In the Island of Kal-Hi-Pee. In the next street but one, he saw other things done Which puzzled his notions of right,— A street-vendor "copp'd " for "just having stopp'd His truck, with a peeler in sight;" While, over the way, in the broad light of day, He saw traffic in infamie— Dtba,sement intense, shocking every sense— Unmolested in Kal-Hi-Pee. Next he went to the House where assembled the nous Of the nation, for public work, • And it staggered him quite to obierve the fierce fight' The Oats made the Ire' life to bark; How net one, if he could, for the national good, Would spare his opponent,—not he!— And he marverd if this was regarded as bliss By the people of Kal-Hi-Pee. After that, he soon found his way to the ground

Where the finest race-horses are run, With their jockeys skilled, and their paces drill'd, And their satin coats bright in the sun; And he thought it no sin that the best horse should win For his owner much E s. d.; But he heard people say, that was not quite the way They ran horses in Kal-Hi-Pee. To the Court of a Beak he next went to seek Illustrations of legalite— How infallibly Law its dispassionate claw Lays on all kinds of rognerie ; And he heard the Beak mild give two months' to a child For plucking a pear off a tree, And three months' to her brother, who'd lull smashed his mother— That was justice in Kal-Hi-Pee. Ta a Church next he went, Oil inquiry bent, The incumbent expecting to see, But the curate slim did the work for him Far a very trifling fee; And Lord B. was told that a great deal of gold That parson made annualie Cut of three or four fat livings—or—mere In the Island of Kat-Hi-Pee. An Art Exhibition, he thought 'twas his mission, To visit inaubitablie,— 'T gas the abow of the year, where the work would appear Of the Princes of Arti:trie; But of great works scarce one the princes had done, Only portraits unlimiteulie, And their High School of Art was, he foand, a mere mart, In the Island of Kal-Eli-Pee. To the theatre next he went, but perplex'd And very unhappy was he, To find a wild craze for stage-carpenter'd plays With fabulous scenerie Was ruling the roost; for he thought it at most, Not a little derogatorie ; But he hoped they would grow, in time, better to know, In the Island of /Cal-Hi-Poe.

LITERARY.—In consequence of recent indiscretions, journalistic, fictional, and poetic, it is thought desirable to appoint a Public Bowdleriser. It is believed that he will be attached to the Excise Department. Zootoor.--.(lt appears to be coming to that at the Board Schools.)—Examiner (to small aspirant to the Twenty-fourth Standard) : Can you tell me anything peculiar about the cuckoo, in regard to nesting ? Student: Yes, sir. Please, sir, he don't lay his own eggs hisself, sir ! OVERHEARD AT A COW/MT.—First Victim: Eugh ! That tenor's top notes are simply atrocious.—Second. Ditto : I call them criminal.—First Ditto: Do you mean that he is chargeable with "uttering false notes ?"--Second Ditto: Worse than that—with committing "murder on the high C's !" "SOUND IN WIND," &C.—lndignant Purchaser (riding in) : I've brought this horse back. He makes a noise when he gallops. He's a confirmed roarer !—Dealer: Well, I never said he wasn't !—lndignant Purchaser: Then, sir, I should like to know what the deuce you meant by warranting him psigt to ride? (Blokey and Son) : Ah ! and wouldn't it do one's 'art good to see "Blokey and Son's Pickles" printed right across it in capital letters, big enough for all the world to read with the naked hi!

div.head: LirrLE TOMMY ON GHOSTS.
div.p: LirrLE TOMMY ON GHOSTS.

These Ghostes, it seems, are like little boys, who they say, "should be seen and not heard." That is, they don't speak, but they stamp and clank chains, which seems regular right down absurd. For if they can glare, and goggle, and make shindies, and rattle among doorways and dishes, Why can't they speak up like spirits of spirit, and just tell us their wants and their wishes? That's why I don't believe in 'em, though they frighten me awfully! This does seem ri-dik-u-lus, rather; But I find it's precisely the same with the grown-ups. For instance, there's Billy Bumps's father, He pooh-poohs all Ghostes, in a big bouncing voice, and • says they're all nerveses and liver; Yet when uncle Jack was a telling of 'em, on Christmas Eve, I could see that he was all of a shiver, Mr. Bumps, I mean and his face went the colour of a na , pan of ski•milk in our dairy, And when he was a-going he run against someone in the passage, and he shrieked, and it was only our Mary. That's how it seems with everyone. These Ghostes are too stupid to believe in, but they do make you creepy, And—l'm almost quite afraid to go to bed after all this, , though I'm awfully, aalully sleepy !

great writer says: "A man ought to carry a pencil and note down the thoughts of the moment." "Yes." remarks a Yankee editor; "and one short pencil devoted , exclusively to that uso would last some men we know about two thousand years, and than have the original I point on." • BLOWING THE BALL.—The winter season calls into re- quest games for round parties. Here is a very simple one, of German origin, known as "The Ball of Wool." The party'are seated round a table, from which the cloth ' must be drawn. A little wool is rolled up into the form of a ball, and placed in the middle of the table. The , company then commence to blow upon it, each one try- ing to drive it away from his own direction, and the ob- ject of all being to blow it off, so that the person by whose right side it falls may pay a forfeit. The longer the ball is kept on the table by the opposing puffs of the surrounding party the more amusing the game becomes, as the distended cheeks and zealous exertions of the players afford mirth to onlookers as well as to them- I selves. Similar to this is.o, game called "Blowing the ' Feather," in which a small feather set floating in the air answers the same purpose as the ball upon the table. The forfeit is paid by the individual whose puff in inef- fectual in keeping the feather afloat, or who suffeis it to drop when it reaches him.

Messrs. Gudgell and Simpson had the best youltg animal at Chicago fat stock show the other day, in the shape of a yearling polled steer. It is said that Mr. Stephenson's black polled heifer "Luxury," champion of the Smithfield Club show, was sold to a London butcher for £l5O, or, roughly speaking, at about 2s. 6d. per lb. The Hon. M. H. Cochrane, of Hillhurst, Canada, is es- tablishing a herd of red Aberdeen polled cattle, which now numbers eleven head, and which is supposed to be the only herd of the kind in the world. The Shorthorn cow, " Thorndade Rose 24t1i,",f0r which Mr. H. Y. Attrill, of Goderich, Ont., paid 500 guineas, at the Audley End sale, and her heifer calf, have reached the stock farm of her owner.

33 You now see the farmer after getting 10 per cent. reduc- tion is short of seed for the next sowing, and giving all his time, his workmen's labour, manure, horse labour, &c., has to put his hand into his pocket for 3 quarters of a bushel to sow with. This injtistice has nearly gone the length of its tether; the cup of the farmer's suffering is full, and the landlord, who has been reaping an ex- traordinary golden harvest, has exacted the last farthing, and has sent already 600.000 agriculturalists from the soil to the great injury of the nation. It is very easy to see that the cause of our present depression comes from landlord oppression, and if the landlords of their own free will will not do justice, the nation must in its own interest do it for them. Farmers ought to send to Parlia- ment men who will represent justice to them and the nation. In conclusion. 33 per cent, should be per- manently reduced from the rent so as to carry a:reduc- tion of the rates before justice can be approached.; also the unjust overdrafts drawn on the farmer should be given back in a tangible form, either by taking no rent or part rent, or what would, in most cases be acceptable to both farmer and landlord, namely, quantities of manure, bought cheap by the landlord, and given to the farmer until the farmer has been compensated for the overpaid rent. The general public would gain most by the latter method, and have a right to gain, for I can easily prove they have suffered much both in quantity and quality of produce from the land through the farmer having no means to buy manure and pay for more labour."

A proposal has been made to have in America a national show of Jersey cattle. The project has been spoken of in the American Jersey Cattle Club, and will probably be again brought formally before them. The American Oxford Down Association have been discussing matters. Members agreed on the good qualities of the Oxford, and expressed much encoprage- meat in raising the breed. They thought America was better adapted to the growth and improvement of the Oxford than its home country, England. The sales for the past year had been very large, good prices prevailing in spite of the general depression, and the future out- look was all that could be desired. THE MIDDLEMAN.—An important meeting of landed proprietors and influential farmers has been held in Hull I for the purpose of starting a co-operative cempany, whose object would be to supply the public direct with meat and farm produce, dispensing with the need of butchers and ether middlemen. The project was taken I up enthusiastically, and a committee was appointed to prepare a report for presentation at a future meeting. The promoter of the scheme, Mr. P. Saltmarslie, of Salt- marshe, presided, and suggested that the company be one with limited liabilities, embodying a capital of £3,000, a considerable proportion of which should be made up of £1 shares. GALLOWAY Cerree.—Galloways have many of the 'characteristics of Aberdeen-Angus cattle, but are some- what smaller, and do not mature at so early an age. ' They are, however, perhaps a little hardier in constitu- tion, and have more hair, whieh is rougher and not so smooth to the touch as that of the Aberdeen-Angus breed, to which they are allied in blood. The prevailing colour of Galloways is black with a brown tinge on the top of the hairs, and, according to Professor Wallace, they have sometimes white spots on the belly, especially where dis- tinct families are crossed. They have stron,ger bones, coarser necks, longer quarters, and the head is not so pointed at the poll as in the case of the sister breed. When crossed with Hereford or Shorthorn, the offspring is excellent for yielding prime beef, but the breed in its pure state is not quite up to the average as milkers. ENSILAGE FOR SHEEP.—Experiments in feeding en- silage to sheep seem to prove that during a number of years past, several parties have spoken of the satisfac- tory results obtained from such feeding. One gentleman from Chatham, New York, had fed ensilaged maize to ewes, before and after lambing, with evident benefit. In America ensilaged maize, rye, and clover have been fed to sheep much more extensively than they heve been In this country, and have met with warm approval there. Lord Walsingham's celebrated flock of South Downs has been largely fed with ensilage for a number of years; and his agent, Mr. Henry Woods, has published valuable pamphlets, giving favourable results of the practice. It was there found profitable as compared with customary foods. Sheep require a variety of food in winter, and roots have been found to conduce to health and thrift when fed with hay, straw, and grain. Unfortunately, roots involve a great deal of labour in their successful cultivation and storage, and if ensilage can take their place, a great saving in labour will be gained. It has been found to brine ewes to lambling in good condition, and it causes an abundant flow of milk afterwards. The only question now seems to be as to the possible danger of its long-continued use as the chief food. Evidently there can be but little danger if hay and other foods- are also used in reasonable proportion. Ensilage wiil pro- bably become an important article of food in producing early lambs for the butcher. WINTER FOOD FOR Cows.—A correspondent writes : " Your readers are often asking the best food for milk- ing cows during winter. Though mine is an arable farm, I milk largely during winter. I proceed as follows We have our cows entirely under cover or in the yards, for the warmer they are kept the less food they want and the more milk they will give. We give no hay; barley and oat straw are cut into chaff about an inch long. Then, again, we go little to market, but convert all our second-rate corn into suitable food; to mix with the chaff. Wheat or barley are boiled ; they may be mixed or used separately. Put five bpshels to about 100 gallons of cold water, and boil till the corn will mash if squeezed in the fingers, then spread chaff enough for a day's allowance for your cows, and put the boiled corn while hot, and mix. We find five bushels sufficient each day for about 40 cows when roots are plentiful; or, if oats are used, they should be crushed. We find these valuable for milk. Of all green foods I like cabbage; and we manage so as to keep a supply all through the winter. Turnips or swedes when they have not been frosted, and up to Christmas, may be used in small quantities with- out injury to the milk. In all cases they should be pulped and mixed with the chaff. - After Christmas, where mangolds are grown, they may be used with Out stint; but it must be borne in mind that they produce a lot of poor milk, therefore the corn should be increased. If a little hay can be spared, give them a little the last thing; but we rarely get any to spare, and when I have used it I have found very little advantage in doing so.' How TO HANDLE CAMPS AND BULLS.—A Baltimore correspondent writes :—" Farmers may find how I handle calves and bulls interesting. I allow them all the milk they want for three weeks, when I put it into a trough for them; after a few days I add a little skim milk (sweet) to it, and I keep on increasing the skim milk until it is all skim milk, when I add a little corn meal or bran. If one of the calves should be behind the rest, I give it a raw egg now and then, which helps it along wonderfully. In the spring I turn the calves into short pasture, but still feed them night and morning. If I raise a bull, I treat him the same until he is eight months old, when I separate him from the heifers, and tie him about in fence corners and small patches, mov- ing him and giving him his feed, a pint of meal night and morning, with an occasional egg. When 15 months old, I turn him with the heifers, and he is treated the same as they are—driven to the field and home with them, tied up and handled the same. With the above treatment, I never had a Jersey or Alderney bull that my boys from four to ten years old could not handle until the bull was. five years old, when I always castrate and kill him. I never had a bull that I had to ring. The only trouble they ever gave was breaking down fences or upsetting them, when I would put a board on their horns, which, when once put on, would remain there as long as they lived. • CHURCII " LIVINGS " LANCA- . SHIRE. "A Northern Churchman," calls attention to "one abuse • in the Church which stands out as a most glaring injus- tice, and which is found much more frequently in the north, where until 150 years ago population was so sparse and parishes of such large dimensions, than in the south- ern province." It is that, he says, where, owing to in- crease of population, the 'value of a living has greatly increased the whole of the increased value is still allowed to remain attached to the mother church, while the daughter churchs receive no benefit from this increase , of value, though this increased value is itself entirely due to the increase of population, which has rendered the • erection of these daughter churches necessary. In some cases the residuary parish attached to the mother church contains only a tenth of the whole population of the parish, and yet the mother church retains the whole of the endowment, so that nine-tenths of the population are prevented benefiting by the great increase in the value of the parish endowment-in other words, are year by year robbed of their right of Sharing in an endowment which belongs to the whole parish. I will take a few instances from Lancashire which are suggestive:- Value. Popula- Benefice. Patron of Benefice. £ tion. 1. Warrington R Lord Lilford 2,000 2. Winwick H Earl of Derby 3. Wigan R. Earl of Bradford 4. Standish R Present Rector 2,500 5. Bury R Earl of Derby 6. Prestwich R Earl of Wilton 1,950 7. Bccleston H Mr. W. Bretherton 1,545 8. Halsall R Mr. H. H. Blundell. 3.500 9. Walton R Mrs. Leigh 3,000 10. West Derby R Present Rector 2,500 11. Liverpool R Present Rector 2,000 12. Leyland V Present Vicar 13. Chorley H The Master Facaily 1,042 14. Croston R Rev. G. S. Molter 1,093 15. Burnley R Present Rector 3,000 , 16. Lancaster V Mr. G. Martin 1,824 , 17. Stockport E Present Rector 2,200 18. Sephton B Marquis de Rothwell 1,824 Walton is the mother church of Liverpool, and includes the northern portion of that great city. It has both a rector and vicar, and A. B. Forwood, some three years I ago, stated that the rectory and vicarage betVireen them I were worth £B.OOO a year. Population is increasing I • , enormously on that side of Liverpool. West Derby in- ' • I eludes the eastern portion of the city of Liverpool. I 1. The parish of Warrington contains eight daughter •I parishes. Two of these (Burton Wood and Padgate) are • of the value of £lO5 and £l3O respectively. , 2. Winwick has 11 daughter parishes, and 10 out of • the 11 have an average income of £220. For the last , century and a half the incumbent has always been a , member of the Stanley family, either by birth or by mar- . riage. The value of the living is very often stated by , L residents in the neighbouroood to he £4,000 a year. , I 3. Wigan has 16 daughter parishes, most of them of ; the regulation value of £3OO-made up to this amount by the Ecclesiastical Commissioners,-but there are four 11 with incomes from £l4O to £l6B. The total population 'I of the oldiparish of Wigan is over 100,000, but the rec- tor's residuary parish only contains some 4,000 people, L and yet has the whole of the endowment attached to it, with the exception, it is believed, of two sums of £5O . I • a year each, paid to two of the incumbents of daughter I parishes in the borough. For very nearly a century and 'L I a half the rectory has been filled by members of the Earl , of Bradford's family. 4. Standish, which has three daughter parishes, with . incomes ranging from £l4O to £l6O, is said to owe its 11 great wealth to royalties from mines. 5. Bury has 16 daughter parishes' (and five of these , under £175 a year) and a total population of over 100,000. , 6. Prestwich is a veritable "plum," from a social and , intellectual point of view, some five miles from Man- , I chester Exchange, and surrounded by the homes of many , of the wealthiest Manchester merchants. The great ; borough of Oldham, with its 150,000 people, forms part • of this parish, and is said to receive £320 a year as its share of the endowment. I 7. Eccleston has two daughter parishes, values £l2B r and £137. It has just been sold, and the old rector has ' resigned. Mr. Bretherton, who has bought it, has ap- pointed to the benefice his son, the Rev. H. W. Brether- I ton, 8.A., who was ordained only the year before his I institution. 8. Flalsall has three daughter parishes-viz., Lydiate, • Melling, and Maghull, stated in the "Diocesan Calendar" ' as being worth £l7O, £ll4, and £144 respectively. • ,9. Lancaster has 16 daughter benefices, most of them ; under £2OO a year, and only one over £250; while Stock- I port has 18 daughters, and of these 8 possess less than , £2OO a year and only one or two above the regulation £3OO a year. , I In such cases as Winwick, Wigan, &c., the natural course would be to reduce the living to say £l,OOO or £1,200 a year, and capitalise the remainder ot the income each year. Thus, in the case of Winwick, £2,000 might each year be placed as a capital sum to the credit of the ' daughter churches-or, in other words, four of these I churches might each year be increased by the interest of £5OO placed to their account in the hands of the Eccle- siastical Commissioners. Oh, what a change would quickly be wrought by such a righteous restoration of the parishoners' rights in the endowment, such rights being now wholly sacrificed to those of the patron!

•• EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. EXPECTED ATTACK ON THE ARABS. CAIRO, SUNDA.Y.—Ahtned Mukhtar Pasha, accompanied by Nubar Pasha, Mr. Cartwright, and Mr. MacDonald, at-- rived here this afternoon, and were received at the railway station by Sir IL 1). Wolff, Mr. Egerton, and the Briish and Egyptian civil and military authorities. His Excellency, 'accompanied by 'Sir H. D. Wolff and Nubar Past4a, im- mediately proceeded to the Istmailia Palace. Lieutenant- . Genrral Sir F. St.phenson has arrived at Akasheh. An attack en the enemy in his intrenched position near Roshell has been decided upon„ Ten surgeons and one

_ Chaplain have been telegraphed for. ABASHER, MONDAY.—Heavy fighting is expected to take Place on the Nile. General Stephensoni who has command of the forcf:s, intentied to check the rebel advance on the British positfms at Kosheh and Akasheb, arrived yesterday at the latter place with his Staff. It is understood that General Stephenson is invested with almost unfettered Powers in deaAng with the enemy; and it is believed he will attack the Arabs in their intrenchrnents opposite Firkeh and Kosheli. The enemy near the latter place have, according to the reverts from Dongola, been recently rein- forceb by some 15 000 mr•ra. There are at Kosheh 600 men ef the Cameron Highlanders and a few cavalry, under the sommand of Colonel St. Leger. rAt Akasheh there are Dearly 1,400 men, composed of detachments of various regiments, besides a small cavalry force. At Wady Haifa there are now nearly 1,000 men, the position having been reinforced. At Assouan and Kraosko there are strong gar- risons, part of which have been mewed to the front for Asaiout, consisting of some six thousand men, including Three or four squadrons of the 20th Hussars, a battery of Royal Artillery, and several battalions of infantry. this advanced force having its base at Assonan numbers nearly 8,500 men, and reinforcements are now on tbe way to join it. The railway being extended to Akasheh offers an alternative route to the Nile for conveying troops forward. GREAT BA.TTLE. DEFEAT OF THE ARABS. THE ESCAFE OF FATHER BONONII FROM KHARTOUM. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY, 2-45 P.T.S.—LieUten int Sir Frederick Stephenson telegraphs .from Kosheh at 11 a.m. to•day, as follows :—I attacked the enemy at six o'clock this morning, "-and occupied Ginniss at nine o'clock. The enemy is now ,!•e,ln full retreat. Our cavalry is still beyond Attab in pur- suit. The enemy's loss was heavy. We captured two guns and twenty banners. Lieutenant Soltan, of the let batta- lion of the Royal Berkshire Regiment, was killed, and Lieutenant Wigan, of the Same regiment, was slightly wounded. Twenty men were also wounded. The loss amoug the Evyntian troops was three officers wounded, Six men killed, and ten men • injured. The health and • spirits of the troops are excellent. RordE, WEDNESDAY.—Kther Bonomi, the Italian priest, Who lately made his escape from Khartoum, where be had ''been kept prisoner by the Mandi, has not succeeded in car- '? Tying out his intention of returning to the Soudan. He Started for Dongola, but was obliged by the approach of the hlandists to rctrace his steps. Tue Vicar-Apostolic at - Cairo has written to the Propganda Fide that he cannot Obtain any news of the Italians who were still detained at -Khartoum when Father Bonomi escaped.

The Government on Wednesday received a long despatch from General Sterihensoe on the Nile, giving details of an important battle fought by his force against the rebels at Gimniss, which was the entrenched forward position of the rebels threatening Akasheh and Kosbeh, the forward Britisk positions on the Nile. By the account given by the General, the fight was a most important one, arid the rebels were com- pletely defeated and put te flight. General Stephenson, with a division and two small brigades, numbering about 3.000 men, moved out from the neighbourhood of Ferket early in the morning, and attacked the Arab entrenchments at Ginniss,s, which were successfully carried after severe fighting. The rebel force numbered about 12,000 men. The British casualties include one officer (Lieut. Saltoun) and 24 men killed, and a number of wounded. The enemy's guns and standards were captured. General Stephenson, in his official telegram to the War Office, says he attacked the enemy at 6 a.m., and' occupied G-innis at 9-15 a.m. The enemy were in full retreat, pursued by the cavalry. The enemy's loss was heavy. Oar casualties were Lieutenant Saltoun (Berkehire Regiment) killed, Lieut. Wigan (Berk- shire) slightly wounded, and 20 men wounded. The Egyp- tian troops had three officers woundcd, six men killed, and ten men wounded. The Press Association says later accounts of the engage- ment show that the British casualties were much less than at first reported, when they were stated to number 24 men killed. Ginnie, the scene of the engagement, lies two miles north of Koshete between that place and Akasheh. General Stephenson's force consisted of from 4,000 to 4,500 men, and his staff included General Grenfell, who commanded a divi- sion, Generals Buller and Huvsbe, each commanding a brigade, and Colonel Ardagh, who superintended the Intelli- gence Department. DETAILS OF THE FIGHTING. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY MIDNIGRT.—Ths following are the details of to-day's engagement between Lieutenant-General Stephenson's troops and the Arabs : The British force left Kosheh at five a.m. The first brig- ade, under Brigadier-General Butler, made a sweep of three miles into the desert towards the south-east, while the British cavalry and the Camel Corps were to the left, and the third brigade, under Colonel liareshe, in echelon, one mile from the Nile. At six o'clock the screw guns opened fire and shelled Kosheh village. The Ist Battalion Cameron Highlanders and a battalion of Egyptian troops then ad- vanced along the river, and carried the village at the point of the bayonet. The enemy made a desperate resistance in their mud houses, and clung to them to the last. After taking the village Colonel Huystie's brigade swung round to the r right and joined the Cameron Highlanders, after which both brigades proceeded to attack the village of Ginniss. - The rebels here made an attack also upon the British, but were unable to withstand the steady advance in line of the two brigades and the heavy artillery fire from the screw guns and camel battery. The enemy, however, bravely charged the first brieade, but were compelled to fall back, and immediately fled in disorder. Five of the Arab emits were killed and fifty of the enemy were found dead in one house. General Butler is now at Attab, and the cavalry beyond Amaral., while Colonel lluyshe's brigade and General Stephention's headquarters are at Ginniss. The armoured steamer Lotus is proceeding up the Nile, and if she can succeed in passing AMaTAT he is expected to cap- ture a number of nuagars. The Lotus proved very useful in co-operating with the British during the attack. The Egyptian troops behaved*well and captured three guns. The Press Association mitierstands that the Government is now prepared to negotiate with the Soudanese rebels for a cessation of hostilities; and it is believed that although the main body of the new Malaili's forces was not encoun- tered on Wednescliy, the leader of the Soudan revolt ill not be opposed to proposals of this kind. No advance to Dongola will be made by the British unless the rebels should again seek to cross the frontier. BULGARIA AND SERVIA. RETURN OF PRINCE ALEXANDER TO SOFIA. REPORTED OUTRAGE AT PIROT. CONSTANTINOPLE, SATURDAY.—The Porte sent a Circular to the Powers yesterday asking for their aid in concluding a definite peace between Servia and Bulgaria. It intimates that in its opinion Servia ought to pay an indemnity, and points out that the maintenance of the armistice entails enormous expense upon Turkey. Soria, SATURDAY.—Prince Alexander made his entry into the capital to-day on his return to kirot, at the head of biz

regiments of infantry, one regiment of cavalt y, and three batteries of artillery. The town was gaily decorated wilte flags, and two triumphal arches had been erected, one at the entrance to the town, bearing the inscription Honour and glory to the victors," the other, near the Palace, inscribed, Slivnitzi," "Dragoman,' " Tsaribrod," "Picot." The Prince and the troops met with an enthrieimtic reception, and were loudly cheered by the people. To-night the town is illuminated. BELGRADE, SATURDAY—The Servian troops evacuated Bulgarian territory. The Bulgarians. it is etated, jinn-fedi- etely advanced as they retired, and occupied the whole territory of Bregora, Adlieh, and the banks of the Timok. This action, it is pointed out-here, constitutes an infringe - meat of the provision contained in the armistice stipu- lating that the troops of either country are Hot to ec- cupy the evacuated territory until five days after the with- drawal SOFIA, MONDAY The Bulgarian Government has ad-1 dreesed.a Note to the Great Powers with regard to the aets, .of aggression recently committed by the Servians. The Note concludes by requesting the good offices of the Great Powers, through whose intervention the suspension of hos- tilities,and the conclusion of an armistice were 'effected, in order that complete satisfaction may be given to the Bul- garian troops by Servia, who, the Note says, wishes to re- new the tactics which she employed before the declaration ef war. The Servians entered Pirot yesterday, before the expiration of the delay fixed by the Commission, and fired upon the Bulgarian gendarmes who were left there to do police duty. wounding two ef them. The Bulgarian com- mander, after protesting against the act, withdrew from the town. Many families who resided in Picot have emigrated to Bulgaria. BELGRADE, MANDAY. It is announced that the Bul- garian tioops have completely sacked Pirot, and have car- ried off even the large bell of the church. The inhabitants state that these acts of devastation took place just before the Bulgarians •evacuated the town King Milan, in the name of the Crown Prince, his given 5,000 f. to be distribu- ted among the poorer inhabitants. A Royal uke.ee has been issued ordering the suspension of the ordinary law in -f?: t.

the district se 'iros. THE EVACUATION OF WIDDIN. SOFIA, THrusDAY.—The commander of the Bulgarian troops at Widdin telegraphs officially that the Serviane com- pletely devastated the Widdin district on evacuating it. Apart from the looting committed by the troops, the Ser- vian military authorities requisitioned from each village 50 sheep, 4 oxsn, 3,000 okes of maize, and 2,000 of wheat, all of which the villagers themselves were forced to convey to Zaitchar and Geotin. . THE Fat NCH PRESIDENCY—MtION OF M. •.- -GREVY.—DISORDERLY SCkNE. PARIS, MONDAY.—The members of the Right nie.t to-day and drew up e resolution aslsing the Congress to adjourn for a month on•the ~round that France is not entirely repre- sented, the departments of Corsica, Lez&-e, Arache, and Landes lseing without Deputies, owing to invelidations of the recent electiors. MM. Michelline, Basly, Lansnerre,' Clovis Hugues,sand four other Extreme Deputies signed a resolution asking that Congress should transfer its power& to a Constituent Assembly, which should be elected with the sole mission of framing a nsw Republican Constitution, without a Presidency and without a Senate. The National Assembly (which consists of the United Chamber of Repre- sentativee and 'Senate) opened at quarter-past one this after-. DODD amidst indescribsble tumult. Foreseeing that attempts would be made to bring propositions before the Congress, he President had the tribune guarded by ushers. This rritated beat the isight and the Extreme Left. Before the sitting was declared open the tumult began. "It is an assembly of usurpers," said a Bonapartist. "It is an illegal Congress," said M. Cassignac ; " four departments are wanting: It is not a Congress, but a den of brigands." M. Kerdrel 'asked for leave to speak and to read the resolution of the Right. The Presi- dent refused, esyinss that an Assembly was merely an else-- torsi college, and that all discussion would be irregular. M. Keedrel then tiled to force his way to the tribune, but the ushers prevented him amid an, immense tumult. The President threatened to suspend the sitting. M. Micheline demanded access- to the tribune, And the uproar increased, the interruptions GUN. CasSagnac and the Right being very violent. The President remained firm, and proceeded to constitute the Assembly simply for the election of a Presi- dent of the Republic. M. Micheline protested, and left the. Assembly. Members of the Right again tried to force the. tribune. At two o'clock voting by roll call le,gen. At the first call the Right. didemt yote, ,hut withdrew in a-body. They met in the eleventh Bureau and decided to abstain en , masse. The roll call was finished at 3-30, and the second roll call then began. The members of the Right, with a few exceptions, abstained from voting, but interrupted the read- of the minutes ; and so ,the Congress ended noisily with the isroclareation of this result t-589 voters, absolute majority 289 ; M. Gravy, 457 votes ; M. Brisson, 68; M. Freycinet. 15; various, 26. M. G:evy was declared elected for seven years. In 1879, out of 670 votes, M. 'Grevy obtained 563 .votes, and Gent. Chauzy 99. M. Brisson is understood to persist in'arefusing to form a new Cabinet. Peens, MONDAY.—The second ballot returns of the elec- tions for the aspartment of the Seine are now almost com- plete. They show that the Radical list has been elected with front 172,000 to 154.000 votes. The Opporturists polled from 104,000 to 93.000, and the Conservatives from 83,000 to 81,000. THE FRENCH MINISTRY. PARIS, THURSDAY, 5 P.M.—ereSideHl Gievy accepted M. Brisson's resignation last evening, and this morning sum- moned M. de Freycinet to request him to undertake the for- mation of a Cabinet. Several of this evening's papers state. that M. de Freycinet showed some reluctance in view of the gravity of the situation. He asked for time to consider the mettEr, and consult his friends and the principal leaders of the Republican majority. • OPERATIONS IN BURMAH.

The following is from the Viceroy "Calcutta, Friday.—The suppression of British Burmah dacoits is proceeding satisfactorily. The troops and police have driven them from Shwegyin, Myitkho, Sittang, and Wimpsdaw, inflicting considerable loss, and taking 70 pri- soners. Toe dacoita are very badly armed, and give little trouble when met. We have lost one villager killed, and a few men slightly wounded. There is some dacoity in the Syriam division, which is being promptly suppressed. The force here is believed to be ample for all requirements. Telegraph communication with Shwegyin has been re- tored." ANNEXATION OF UPPER BURMAIL—IMPERIAL PROCLAMATION. The following proclamation will be issued to-day by the Viceroy and Governor General of India : "Ey command of the Queen-Empress, it is hereby noti- fied that the territories formerly governed by King Thebaw will no longer be under his rule, but have become part of Her Majesty's dominions, and will during Her Majesty's pleasure be administered by such officers ae the Viceroy and Governor Genera! of India may from time to time appoint. (Signed) " DUFFEILIN." THE CONGO STATE. BRUSSELS, MONDAY.—The Congo State has adopted the personal arms of the King of the Belgians. to which has been added the symbolical star of the Congo flag. The de- vice is " Trayap et progress." The Belgian Press censure I severely the administrators of the Congo State for their ! Present mystery-mongering. The convention concluded *it h an English syndicate for the construction of the Congo railway was for everybody in Belgium a surprise. Very large concessions of land are said to have been secured for the company to be formed by the syndicate. The principal Belgian statesmen, it should be Observed, have never ap- proved of the Congo enterprise, and have always kept aloof from it. THE QUEEN OF SPAIN AND THE LEGISLATURE. MADRID, SATURDAY.—The session of the Cortes was opened by Royal decree, which was read by Senor Sagasta, the Premier, in both Houses. In the Congress Senor Canovas del Castillo was elected President by 222 votes against 112 recorded for Senor Romero y Robledo. Senor Canovas subsequently delivered a patriotic speech from the chair, in the course of which he referred to the late King in terms of admiration and respect, amid applause from the deputies. He urged upon all parties to unite for the de- fence of peace and legal institutions, so as to avoid the dangers of anarchy and the disasters of civil war. At the conclusion of the President's speech a deputy exclaimed, 'Long live the Queen Regent!" the cry being taken up and redeated by the other members. It was then unani- mously decided that a deputation should proceed to the Palace to express to Queen Christina the great regret of the Chamber at the death of King Alfonso. A similar resolution eras unanimously passed in the Senate. SOUTH AFRICA. FIGHTING BETWEEN THE BOERS AND NATIVES. WOMEN AND CHILD.

; KEN KILLED. CAPETOWN, DEC. 9.—The following loan account by an eve-witness of the fight which occurred at Marnusa on the 2nd inst. between the Boers under General Joubert and Mas- souw's natives. General Joubert with about 900 Boers sur- rounded a kopje held by Massouw and 100 natives. Some of the Boers advanced and informed the natives that they had come to disarm them Ode Boer seized a native's gun, and a struggle ensued, during which the gun accidentally went off, whereupon the remaining Boers opened a heavy fire on the Kaffirs, who fled on to the flat at the foot of the kopje and were shot indiscriminately without regard to age or sex. About 30 natives and 40 women and children were I shot, while nine Boers were killed and 14 wounded. Of these only three are said to have been killed by the natives, tlie remainder being killed by the cross firing of the attack- ing force. Their supply of water running short the natives surrendered after bolding out twentv-four hours. Mas- souw was found to have been shot dead. Several English- men who gave water to wounded natives were insulted by the Boers.

The latsst intelligence from Basutoland is of a satisfac- tory nature, everything being quiet in the principal dis- tricts. The Governor of Cape Colony has arrived at Port EFzi- beth to open the South African Exhibition. The ceremony takes place to-nvirrow. His Excellency's reception was re- ectful but not demonstrative. During the week no further fighting was reported from l'ondoland, bnt it is stated that an impi of 300 Pondos is marching on Rhode for the purpose of exterminating 7:eta's people.

_ TITE COLLIERY DISASP:RTAI, &Juni: WALES The number of victims through the appalling colliery dieter in the Rhondda Valley had on Tuesday reached 78, three of the men having died of their irijuriee. The work ef burying the dead was begun on Saturday morning, many of the hodies having been removed by relatives of the deceased before the arrival of the Coroner, who subetquently offered an explanation of the delay which had occurred in the opening cl the inquest. After the jury had been sworn, an intimation was given that after the identification of tbse bodies which remained, the inquiry would be adjourned tii3 January 12th. The certificates for burial were then handed e by the Coroner to such relatives who had come down the valley to Ferndale to meet him. Some of these poor people broke out into loud sobs on taking these documents in their hands. The jury then proceeded under the directien of the Coroner to view the bodies remaining at Mardy, as well as two or three lying at Ferndale- Newly-made biers stood at short distances from each other along the few streets, and round them gathered groups of friends of the deceased men, and crowds who had come up the valley or crossed the hills daring the forenoen. One by one the bodies were carried oat. The ministers of Mardy, assisted by brother pastors from neighbouring villages, went from group to group, read to each a few verses ef scripture, offered up a fervent prayer, and led them in the singing of a hymn. The whole service was in Welsh, and I was moat deeply impressive, especially the singing, for the tune was plaintively sad, and was sung with quivering voices. Widows, mother, and sisters, whose grief has hitherto been concealed in the privacy of their homes, were , new led out or clothed its Mourning, the simplicity of which was sometimes touchingly suggestive of their poverty. IThe men had, in many cases, long black bands tied round ' their hats, or black sashes looped round their shoulders, buts great many were forced to come in their ordinary off-work clothes. One by one the biers were lifted on the shoulders' of the men, and borne away down the valley to the ceme- tery lying midway between Mardy and Ferndale. The road is uneven, and has only recently been covered with new macadam. The bearers had consequently to be frequently relieved, for the way was long as well as bard. No one could look on the scene unmoved. Twenty-one corpses fol- lowed each other at intervals in a long procession with a wreath or two on the lid of each coffin, succeeded by the long train of weeping women and more composed, but still deeply distressed, men ; and the strains of the funeral hymn rising from the village and the cemetery echoed back from the great barren and cold mountains which shut-it the val- ley from the rest of the world. Net nre herself wears a sad aspect np these bleak Welsh villages, and were it not for their coal they would be deserted. On the arrival of each body at the cemetery, there was another short service. The Church of England curates read their order of burial, and the ministers of the many Dissenters offered a prayer and joined in a hymn over each of their flock. Pitmen and labourers did duty, under the direction of the suxtoe,-and dust was committed to dust very reverently. Words of comfort were then spoken to each group of mourners, and ' the people returned to the village. . . Fun rile took place on Tuesday at Mardy and immediate district. Some curious incidents have been brought to light lin connection with the lives of some of the deceased miners. During the hurry tvhich prevailed in earring the dead bodies home on Wednesday night, two bodies, these of father and son, were taken oorne to a house in Hill-street, and deposi- ted on the kitchen floor. The carriers then left hurriedly to convey oilers. It happened that the only persons in the house were the little chitdree of the dead man. His wife had recently eloped with another man, and she was residing at Cwepark. When she heard of the exploeion, it seems that the old affection was re-kin:tied, and over the moun- tains she came, through the darkness, to find the children alone with the dead. In another instance one of those who lost their lives was somewhat addicted to drink, and when under its influence he was in the habit' of using very dis- agreeable expressions towards his wife::•se She had seen bet- ter days, havine been in respectsble service. Tney had two litt'e daughters. Daring one of his drinking bouts she took him at his word, and went away. For two year's he knew not what had become of her. Whenever he heard that someone resembling her had been seen, it did not 'mat- ter how far away, he would proceed thither as quickly as he could. In this way he visited many distant parts of South Wales. One day,' three months ago, he heard she was in Risca, in the service of a lady. He had, however, to come home 'without her. On his way he met a woman, to whom he said, with joy beaming in his eyes, "I have found Ann. I went into the kitchen of the place where she is in service. I saw her jacket banging on the wall, and I felt as though I could eat it." He continued, " I had to wait two hours before she would come to me, and when she did she refused to come home with me." For two 'months he journeyed to Risco frequently, but Ann was still olsclurate. One day a happy thought occurred to him. He dressed their tNo little daughters as well as he could, with a white pinafore and a small turnover on each, and took them to Rises, and no sooner did Ann see her little girls than all was forgiven on the spot, and home together the little family returned. Sad to say, the recon- ciliation had not taken place more than a few weeks when the explosion killed the father. Another man killed was known by the name of " Resurrection Tom." Some .time ago, while employed in another colliery, he induced a friend of his to write to his friends in West 'Wales, stating that he was dead and buried. His friends, knowing that he was is a club, came for the money, and thereby found Torn was alive. The men at Mardy heard the story, and so nicknamed him "Resurrection Tons." The North Wales quarrymen have sent to Mardy proffer- ing assistance in the relief of the sufferers by the recent colliery explosion. The colliery proprietors have given £3OO and Lord Bute £2OO.

THE HOME RULE QUESTION. WHAT THE PARNELLITES WOULD ACCEPT. Mr. Labouchere, M.P., in a letter to the Times, giies it to be understood tbat the following Home Rule scheme would be accepted by Mr. Parnell and his followers :- 1. Representation in the Imperial Parliament upon Impe- rial matters alone—This would re quire a hard and fast definition as to what is Imperial and what islocal, toge- ther with, as in the United States, some legal tribunal of appeal. The Army, the Navy, the protection of the British Isles, and the commercial and political relations with foreign nations, would be regarded as Imperial nutters, and pro- bably there would be no insuperable difficulty—if it were deemed expedient—in arranging a Customs Union, such as that of the German Zollverein before the German Empire came into existence, leaving it to the Irish to foster, their industries, if they please. by means of bounties. There would be an Imperial Budget, which would be submitted each year to the Imperial Parliament, with the Irish sitting in it. Each country would contribute its quota according to population and property. If more were required, the pro- portions would be maintained. Each island 'would raise its quota as it best pleased. 2. 'The dovernment of Ireland.—A Viceroy, a Privy Coun- cil, a Representative Assembly, Ministers. (1) The Viceroy.—A member of the Royal Family, with a salary of £25000 per annum. (2) Privy Council.—The present Privy ColAncil consists of about fifty individuals, all of them anti-Nationalists, and some of them virulently so. The Council would have to be reorganised. This might be done by nominating 100 new Councillors, men of moderate views, but who would frankly accept the arrangement, and endeavour to give practical effect to it. The Council would gradually be increased by the admission of the Irish Ministers. (3) House of Representatives.—lts members would be elected, as with us, according to population. As a conces- sion, however, it would be agreed that one-fourth of the r members might be nominated, either during two Parliaments or for five years. (4) Ministers.—They would be selected from the Perna- mentry majority, as with us. The Viceroy would call upon the leader of the majority to form a Cabinet. He would, however, retain the constitutional right of the Queen to dis- solve. 3. The veto.—This would be reserved to the Viceroy, with the consent of his Privy Council. Of one thing I am absolutely certain. It is that no arrangement is possible which would give the veto to the Imperial Parliament. The Irish object to this, because they consider that it would con- vert tbeir assembly into a mere debatin4 society. We— although we seem just now enamoured with it—should soon be brought again to a standstill, as we should be perpetually debating Irish bills. The Irish would also object to the Queen exercising the veto by the advice of her Council, for practically this would mean the veto of those representing the majority in the English Parliament. The Privy Connell is, unfortunately, historically odious in Ireland. But were it mecast it is probable that the Irish would not object to the veto which I have suggested. 4. Protection of minorities.—They would already be pro- tected by the veto, by the nominated members, and by the Orangemen, who would return a considerable contingent ; but the Irish would go even further than this. (1) No contract existing or entered into could he set aside by Irish legislation. In the event of anyone feeling him.' self aggrieved in this matter he might appeal to the Judi- cial Committee of the House of Lords.

RUPTCY ACT. • At Warringiorz County Court on Thursday; Mr. P. Dayies';..solicitor, -Warrington, applied' to his Honour Judge Ffoulkes for the discharge 4 Mr. William Porter, builder and contractor, of Warrington, who was recently declared a bankrupt.--The Deputy Official Receiver (Mr. Worsley) handed in a filed statement in which complaint was made that the debtor had continued business when he knew that he was insolvent, and that he had not kept in. his books a profit and loss account. —Mr. Davies said that on the 23rd of March Mr. Porter called a meet- ing of his creditors at Liverpool, at which the whole of his creditors were either present or represented. The statement presented to the meeting, which was verified by an independent valuation, shOwed that the estate was worth considerably more than 20s. in the provided that the property that the debtor then had could be sold for anything near what it cost him. It was also stated that the debtor had a contract with the Bootle School Board, under which, if he became a bankrupt, they had the power to withhold from him, the slim of £1,500, which really belonged to him. It was then agreed, for the benefit of the' creditors, to' accept 20s: in the .£, to be paid in instalments, and Mr. Porter carried on the business simply as a foreman, under the superintendence of the creditors. -- His Honour said that the Bankruptcy Act was passed with a view to have some effect upon the' tra- ding community of the country. The time for which the discharge of a bankrupt should 'l,be' suspended was left. to the discretion of the Court, !And the Court had to be guided by the report of ; the Official Receiver. With regard to that particn- lar case, the greatest complaint was as to the debtor not having kept proper accounts. That was one of the greatest evils, perhaps, that could be, because a man went on without looking his affairs in the face, and did not know, when he was asking credit from other people, how he stood as a trader before the commercial world. At last, owing to an omission of that kind, people who had given him credit found that they were trusting to a straw, and that the person was not in such circumstances as to discharge his liabilities. Thus serious losses were inflicted upon other traders, and it frequently happened that one trader brought down another, and the man brought 'down might be perfectly in- nocent in the matter. In this way distress was spread from one place to another. It was a very important matter indeed that traders should, whatever their business might be, keep proper ac- counts to show how they stood with reference to their own trading transactions. If people did that it would save a great deal of the distross that so frequently occurred in the trading community.. The' debtor in the present case had not made out proper accounts. lie thought that there was ground for suspending the operation of the order ;of discharge for a certain time, and that he would be justified in fixing that time of postponement at two years.-- Mr. Davies mentioned that the creditors were desir- ous that the debtors discharge should not be long delayed, and asked his Honour to reconsider his de- cision.—His Honoitr said that it was not a question , for the creditors, but of the effect that kind of ap- plication had upon the trading community. The object of the Act was to hold out a -warning to people as to a proper and improper mode of trading. He declined to alter his decision.

A COLLIERY ON FIRE.—A serious accident occurred on Tuesday morning at the Taylor Colliery of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, at Shevington. Fire broke out in the pit in consequence of shot-firing, and a number of men wore at work isolating the burning portion by blocking the air-- way which the gas exploded. Fifteen of the men, includ- ing Mr. Hilton, manager of the Hindley Collieries, were severely burnt, and in some cases the injuries are expected to terminate fatally. There were about forty colliers in the pit when the explosion took place, but they escaped unhurt. To avoid further risk of life, it was deckled to flood the part of the mine which was on fire, and operations were at once commenced. GLADSTONE AND DISETABLISHDIENT.—Referring to the actions of the Nonconformists in keeping in abeyance their views of Disestablishment during the recent election, Mr. Gladstone writes :—" Hawarden Castle.—Dear Mr. Newman Hall,—l thank you for your interesting notes. In Scotland, both sides of the Liberal party (so to speak) dis- played self-command and wisdom on the Establishment in question. In England the Nonconformists have once more behaved, towards myself in particular, with a free and generous confidence. I do not think that the mistrust, and even positive hostility, exhibited in some other quarters, whether , more or less limited in extent, have been wise with reference to the interests which it has been sought to defend.—Believe me. dear Mr. Newman Hall, very faithfully yours, W. E.. GLADSrONE." M. CHILDERS SELECTED FOR EDINBURGH—At a meet- ing on Tuesday night of tbe Liberal Committee which se- cured the election of the late Sir G. Harrison for South Edinburgh, Mr. Childers was unanimously adopted as the candidate for the vacant seat. The right hon. gentleman, who arrived in the city oil Tuesday, addressed the meeting, and intimated his acceptance of the invitation. He intro- duced himself as a hard working Liberal member of Parlia- ment for the last 26 years, who had during that time striven to take a part in the great measures promoted by the Liberal party. He appeared now as an earnest supporter of Mr. Gladstone's principles as enunciated in the Midlothian manifesto and speeches. His cMr. Childers's) advice to the Liberal party was " union" in view of the struggle be- fore them in Parliament, and he,,if returned, would hold firmly to the principles which had given so much to. that party in the pest. THE NETHERBY HALL OUTRAGE.—At Carlisle Gaol, On Tuesday, Anthony Rudge, John Martin, and Tames Baker were again charged with burglary at Netherby Hall, at- tempting to murder three police constables in Carlisle, and murdering Constable Byrnes at Phu-lepton. One of the principle witnesses was Constable Fortune, who followed the men along the railway in Carlisle, and was murderously beaten and left for dead, with a score of wounds on his head. Other evidence was given as to the finding in the river at Tebay some portion of the jewellery stolen from Netherbv, and as to Baker having told a fellow prisoner in Carlisle Gaol that the booty was thrown into the water at that place. The prisoners were finally committed for trial at the assizes. The fourth prisoner, also named James Baker, whoewas apprehended in London last week on MS- , picion of having been engaged in the outrage.was discharged , from custody on Tue,sdaye the evidence of his identity being insufficient. DEATH OF THE IRISH PRIMATE.—The Right Hen. and Most Rev. G. M. Beresford, Archbishop of Armagh and Primate of the Irish Church, died on Saturday morning at a quarter past ten, at the Palace, Armagh. Marcus Gervais, Arch ishop of Armagh, was the son of the Bishop of Kil- more. who was a nephew of the first Marquis of Waterford. He was born in 1801, and educated under Dr. Tate at Rich- mond School, whence he proceeded to Trinity College, Cambridge. He served as rector of Kildallen, and Arch- deacon of Ardagh, and in 1854 he became Bishop of Kil- more. In 1863 he was translated to the Primacy, in sue- cession to another Beresford, and he also held the Office of Lord Almoner, and was Prelate of the Order of St. Patrick. Handsome in person, munificent to a degree, courteous and, kindly, he was an excellent specimen of a prelate of the old school. He was a moderate High Churchman and strong Conservative. Of late years his Grace had been in very feeble health, and not able to do much work. FATAL AGRARIAN DISPCTE.—A Most frightful occurrence took place near Larkhill, about seven miles from Newry, on Christmas Day. Three men named John Wetland, Charles fil‘Pariand, his son, and Peter M‘Parland, nephew of the farmer, were seated in a neighbour's house on Christ- mas evening, shortly after four o'clock, with a Rumber of

other farmers, drinking and chatting. As the drink, hew-- ever, commenced to take eßect the conversation turned to a disputed right of way, in which all the M•Parlands are said, to have an interest_ An altercation arose, and Peter MiPar- land, in a fit of anger, is alleged to have lifted a pair of heavy tongs lying before the fire and violently struck,bie uncle, John M`Parland, over the head, inflicting a fearful wound penetrating into the brain, and splitting the skull for several inches over the right ear. The unfortunate man fell to the ground without a murmur. and Charles M•Par-- land is stated to have interfered with Peter as he was- leaving the house. The latter is then alleged to have struck Charles with the tongs over the head several times, rendering him insensible. A doctor was subsequently sent for, but medical skill proved unavailing, and John lelTariand died on Sunday morning, never having regained conscious- ; nese.. The other man is not expected to recover, his head and face being a mass of wounds of a most dangerous char- acter. Peter M'Parland was arrested, taken before a I magistrate, and remanded. SROCEING COLLIERY FATALITY.—On Thursday. MT. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Manor Arms,l Sutton, touching the death of John tietch, 43 years- of age, I who was killed by falling down the shaft of a new pit at the Ashton's Green Colliery, on TueQday. Me. Hall, Government Inspector of Mines, was present. Deceased and a number of other men were engaged sinking the haft, and bad got 380 yards down. At a distance of 100 yards from the bottom there was the mouth of a road- way, and over it was a piece of bratticing to direct the air. down the shaft to the sinkers. By means of a hopnet, 41t. deep and 4ft. fiin, across the top, attached to a flat rope by three hooks, and worked by an engine on the sur- face, the men were raised or lowered. The Cor- oner. in opening the proceedings stafee that de- ceased was employed by a Mr. Piaott, whe was sinking the shaft for Messrs.Bromilow, Foster, and Co.— Aftet William Howard. of Skelmeredale, had identified the body as that of his half-brother, who had worked at sinking pits for thirty years off and cu, Henry Marsh, enginensan, stated that as It was lowered he saw deceased sitting on the side of the hoppet. He was a heavy man, and sat well out of it, with each hand holding a separate chain. It was against the rules to ride in that way, but the deceased did it regularly, and Mr. Pigott must have seen this breach of the rules.—James Carroll, browman, said when deceased 1, was five yards down he let go one chain, and put his hand toll his neck. Witness saw no more. Deceased would never get right into the hoppet.—Thomas Deran, sinker, said he was at the bottom when deceared fell with a great crash. He never spoke, and was quite dead.—Mr. Hall stated that one of the rules particularly statcci that no man should ride on the hoppet. but should be well in-ide. It was very evi- dent. if that rule had been attended to, this accident would not have happened. The Coroner said he did not think he could direct the jury that there was celpable neelect on the part of anybody. Deceased knew as well as anybody else that it was danaerons to ride on the hoppet, and more especie' ly to lot loose with one hand when be was five yards down. He thought the engineman ought to have refused to lower we en be saw the deceased sittina on the side.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and made a presentment thanin future greater care should be exereieed in the enforcement of the rules.
