div.head: EXAMINER
div.p: THE EXAMINER
SATURDAY, JANUARY 2, 1886.

THE Year that has just passed away has been a memorable one in many respects for the people of the United Kingdom. It has been crowded with events, and, especially it would seem, when we look back, with events of a more or less melancholy character. We live faster than of old; and there is more of danger and of disaster, not only because Of this, but because of our ever-increasing popu- lation, and the ever•increasing complexity of the problems of civilisation. We seem as a people, too, to dwell upon our sorrows rather than our joys. A year of plenty and of good trade is taken as a matter of course ; there is a proportionate but unwise expansion of expenditure, and when depression comes we are found, for the most part, unprepared for it. The year 1885 has witnessed a continua- tion of the stagnation in trade which followed upon the abnormal inflation of tell years ago. The great capitalists have been the greatest sufferers; for business has been conducted' in many instances at a loss; while the earn- ings of the masses have been fully up to the average of the past ten years. We are speak- ing now of workpeople as a whole, well know- ing that in some centres of industry there have been little work and considerable distress. Business, if not what is called good, is, there is reason to believe, being conducted on a sound basis. Merchants have grown more strict as to the terms of credit; smaller tradesmen are compelled in consequence to be careful and economical, and there are con- sequently fewer bankruptcies and "private arrangements." One feature of the year 1885 has been the Prominence given for the first time to the Crofters question, for it was on the znd of January that a sheriff's officer was mobbed and assaulted at Glendale. The Bth of the same month witnessed an event of a more agreeable character—that-of the celebration at Sandringham, and other places, of the coming of age of Prince EDWARD, the eldest son of the PRINCE OF WALES—" a King that is to be." On the 26th of January, the ill-starred campaign in the Soudan had its culmination in the death of General GORDON —a circumstance which, when it became known ten days later, profoundly stirred the heart of the nation, for whatever General GORDON'S failings, and he was by no means perfect, it was felt that he was "a creature of hefoic blood," who had perished at what he believed to be the post of duty. February was chiefly noteworthy for the sensation caused by the attempt in the United States ,on the life of O'DoNovAN ROSSA, the head ! centre of the dynamite conspirators. In IMarch we had the commencement of that :difficulty with Russia as to the Afghan frontier which ultimately cost so many millions iii preparations for a war which was averted only by the skilful statesmanship of Lord GRANVILLE and Mr. GLADSTONE. It was on the 13th March that the announcement was made of the agreement of Russia to suspend advances on the Afghan frontier ; and it was on April 9th that news was received in England of the engagement on the frontier between IRussian and Afghan troops. On the 27th !April the House of Commons, after a mag- nificent speech by Mr. GLADSTONE, agreed Ito a Vote of Credit of eleven millions without a word of discussion ; and until May 6th, when negociations took a favourable turn, 'there was no small excitement in the country lat the prospect of a war with Russia. The ' zith of May was remarkable as the day on which the Redistribution of Seats Bill passed ithe House of Commons, and was sent up to the House of Lords. The Franchise Bill, it will be remembered, became law just before Christmas in 184. On May 18th, two of the dynamiters, BURTON and CUNNINGHAM, were , sentenced to penal servitude for life for cans" ing dynamite explosions in London; and on May 22nd M. VICTOR HUGO died in Paris at the ripe age of 82. The death of the great French poet and novelist was followed by the demise, on the sth oi June, of Sir juvus BENEDICT, the eminent musical composer.. Three days later—on the Bth of June—the Conservatives, in conjunction with the Pal-

nellites, were successful, after innumerable assaults, in defeating Mr. GLADSTONE'S Government on a vital issue. It was in the matter of the Budget proposals; Mr. CHIL- DERSI as Chancellor of the Exchequer, sought to provide for paying his way as far as pos- sible by raising the income-tax to 8d in the Pound ; by equalising the death duties'; and by increasing the spirit and beer duties. Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH introduced an amendment which, disregarding the increase in the income-tax, took- exception to the other proposals. In the course of his speech he suggested that there ought to be a further ta:c on tea rather than beer; and on his reso- lution being put to the vote it was carried by a majority of 12, the numbers being 264. for, and 252 against, the amendment. The Government immediately met to consider the situation, and announced their determination to resign. On the 24th June Mr. GLADSTONE surrendered the seals of office. and Lord SALISBURY kissed hands and took charge of them. The Tory Government proceeded with the Budget, but they had nothing to say about taxing tea. They preferred in the traditional fashion to take things easy as to money Matters. What if there was a deficit? It could be met as other Tory deficits had been met—by the next Liberal Government. On the 18th June,while the Government crisis was under consideration, the country was startled, as it was startled last week, by the news of a great colliery disaster, thzet of the Clifton , Hall colliery, near Manchester, which re- sulted in the loss of 178 lives. The 23rd of the next month (July) was distinguished by the marriage at •Whippingham Church, Isle of Wight, of the PRINCESS BEATRICE to PRINCE HENRY of BATTENBERG ; and also by the death of General GRANT, ex-Presi- dent of the United States, and the greatest Soldier of the great Civil War. On the first of August, Louts REIL, the Canadian rebel, Was sentenced to death for high treason ; and on August 6th Lord RANDOLPH CHURCH- ILL introduced an Indian Budget in the House of Commons, the chief feature of which was a deficit of one million and a half, for which he made no provision. The session closed on the r4.th of the same month, Par- liament itself—the tenth of QUEEN VICTORIA —being dissolved on the r6th of November. What is usually spoken of as the Eastern question was revived on the rBth September by the people of Eastern Roum- lia declaring their union with Bulgaria. This led to war . between Servia and Bulgaria, and, as hostili- ties are suspended only, there is no saying how the issue will terminate. On the first day of October Lord SHAFTESBURY died full of years and of honours; and on the 22nd of the same month a shock was given to the nation by the sudden death of Bishop FRASER. On November 25th the KING OF SPAlN—"the gentle Alphonso "—passed gently away; and at home, during November and the early Part of December, the nation underwent the throes of a General Election upon an ex- tended suffrage which has added 2,700,000 voters to the electoral rolls of the country. Such a Reform in the Constitution—a Revo- lution some would call it—is undoubtedly, historically considered, the most important Political event of the year. It is the crown- ing work of Mr. GLADSTONE, and it is gratifying to see that the new electors have shown that they are grateful to, and that they have confidence in, the greatest statesman of modern times.

FRANCE has just passed through another constitutional crisis, and the result is highly satisfactory as tending to show the firm- ness of the basis upon which the Republic is established. Monday was the day for the Meeting of both Chambers for the election of President of the Republic. There was a scene of course; Frenchmen cannot settle a matter of this kind without one. There was a good deal of shouting; some hard words were ex- changed, and there was imminent danger, at one time, of the Deputies Coming to blows; but in the end there was peace. The minority ----the haters of the Republic—retired by way of protest, and M. GREVY was re-elected President by 589 votes. As this is larger than the number by which he was elected seven Years ago, it speaks well for the manner in Which M. GREVY has discharged the import- ant duties of his high office. Frenchmen have shown themselves, in matters poli- tical almost as fickle during the ,Republic

as under the Empire; Governments- have come, and Governments have gone, but M. GREvY has kept his place in the con- fidence of his countrymen. Odd as it may seem. this is because he has shown himself less French than the average Frenchman. He has not excited himself about politics; he has not taken sides with particular mini- sters. The view he has taken of his position has been that of representative of the Repub- lic whatever Government might be in power. He has set an example in this respect which, it is to be hoped, will become constitutional SO far as France is concerned. There is sufficient of turmoil in the see-saw of par- tieewithout having the situation aggravated by the constant interference of a President Who would also be a Ruler. The Chief of a State should always, of course, be strong enough for his post ; but it is hardly likely that a weak man will at any time be selected. The danger is that a strong party man should become President, and that the tide of battle should be incessantly raging round his person. The Republic of the United States suffers in consequence of the struggle for the Presidency being big with fate to office-holders of so many kinds, and to the two great parties in the country. France is broken up into many parties, and, although this state of things has obvious drawbacks, it has its advantages at the time of a Presidential election; for then, as we have twice seen, there is a fusion of those Who would m4intain the Republic as against those who seek to compass its overthrow. Happily the combined forces of the con- spirators against the life of the French Re- public are in such a minority that their case is almost a hopeless one. Frenchmen are not in the most contented mood ; they are dissatisfied with the results of the foreign Policy of the past few years ; and they do not hesitate to display their dissatisfaction by overturning one Ministry after another. But When it comes to a question of choosing between Republicanism and Anti-Repub- licanism they set aside minor grievances, and Cry " Vive la Republique." This we regard as a healthy sign for the future. The Re- public, as M. THIERS said, least divides France ; the longer it lasts the longer it is likely to last.

QUITE a gloom was cast over Warrington early in the week when it became known that two young lovers had been found drowned, on Sunday, in the lock at Mersey Mills. There 18 something inexpressibly sad in such a fate under such circumstances. The youth and maiden were both seventeen—an age when, as in this case, the dawn of love makes life

doubly dear. The season, too, was a festive one. It was the night after Christmas Day when, walking by the river, in the treacherous fog, they made a false step and were en- gulphed in the waters of the remorseless lock. There is no suspicion of foul play, and the chances are that the details of the catastrophe will remain a mystery. It is exceedingly probable that the ill-fated pair were walking arm in arm, and that when the fatal step was made they were dragged down together. Companions who saw them last on oat- urday evening state that the young couple were on good terms; and that LAWSON re- marked, with a jocularity which looks grim in the light of the subsequent tragedy, that "it would look nice if they fell into the river." The night was foggy, and he was conscious that there was some risk of accident; but with the happy carelessness of youth he rade a jest of the danger. He had doubtless gone by the river scores of times, and would think. as the phrase is, that he "knew the road blindfold." But the fog. with .its misleading and spectral effects—he had not thought sufficiently of that, and the terrible penalty of the mistake is the loss of two young lives. It is appalling to find one witness testifying that to his knowledge four persons had been drowned in Mersey Mill lock. So great a sacrifice was surely not needed before taking steps to render it less dangerous to , walk by this part of the river. Mr. JONES, on behalf of the Bridgewater Canal Com- pany, expressed a doubt as to whether there was a legal right of way; but as to this it may be remarked that the presumption is in favour of there being a right of way, , seeing that there is a footpath which is in constant use. But, apart from this, there ' is, as the Coroner justly remarked, a moral , obligation to protect the lives of those who I are permitted, if it be a permission, to walk by the river; and it is to be hoped I there will be no difficulty about carrying out the suggestion of the jury that the foot- path should be protected from Faircloughts Mill as far as the Halfpenny Bridge. It were well the Company did "so much for charity's sake," even if it be not nominated in the bond ; and on the other hand people, young and old, will do well to keep far enough away from the river bank when the extraordinary dangers of fog are added to the ordinary dangers of the dark.
LOCAL NEWS.

RUNCORN NEW BOARD Bosoms will be opened on Mon- day, January 11th. COMPLIMENTARY DINNER TO MR. MUSPRATT.—A COM- plimentiry dinner to Mr. E. K. Muspratt, the Liberal candi- date of the Widnes Division, is to take place at the Reform Club, Liverpool, on the 18th January. THE SUDDEN DEATHS AT WIDNES.—ID the case of the death of Margaret Doyle, wife of John Doyle, labourer, 74, Timperley-street, and her new-born babe, under cir- cumstances reported last week, the coroner thought it un- necessary to hold an inquest. BETHESDA IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.—The mem- bers of this Young Mea's Society bad a social gathering in the school-room on Wednesday evening. Ladies were in- troduced, and a most pleasant and enjoyable evening was spent in dancing and a variety of other ways. A WIDNES Fseatatz.-0a Thursday, at the Liverpool County Cotirt, before Mr. Registrar Cooper, John Hough, estate agent, Widnes, passed his public examination, the official receiver and the trustees of the estate having ex- pressed themselves satisfied with the state of affairs. STORM IN RUNCORN NEIGHBOURHOOD.-011 Monday a storm of considerable fury broke over Runcorn and neigh- bourhood. At both Runcorn and Widnes windows were smashed and slates removed from the roofs of houses, but no serious damage was done. Weston Point, which occupies an exposed position, fared much worse. A portion of the vicarage roof was carried away; a vessel in the new dock broke adrift and was carried across the dock, but was fortu- nately secured before seriously dameged, and the smashing of window Danes and the falling of chimney pots was almost general. PRIM BREAKFAST TO OLD PEOPLE AT PRODSHAM.—Os Christmas morning upwards of thirty old people attended by invitation at the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, Fred- sham, and were entertained to a substantial breakfast. The custom was instituted by the Rev. D. Schofield, when resi- dent minister at Frodsham, and that gentleman was present. and gave a seasonable address. The Rev. T. Lager also made a few remarks, and the choir sang several songs. The aged guests thoroughly enjoyed the good things provided by Mrs.l Lager, Rev. R. P. Berwick, Messrs. William Booth, James Hough, and Philip Darlington. MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN...-.Mr. William Pownall, jun., secretary to the "Y.M.C.A., was at the Parish Church on Tuesday morning married to Miss Owen, daughter of Cap- tain Owen, of Brackley-street, Runcorn. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. T. M. Armson, in the presence of a good congregation. Mr. Joseph Kirkham officiated as best man, and the bridesmaids were Miss S. J. Owen and I Miss Ridyard. Amongst the numerous gifts was a hand- some family Bible presented by the committee of the Y.M.C.A., as an acknowledgment of his labours as secretary during the pat three years. The happy couple are spending the honeyrnodn in London. CHRISTMAS TREE AT WIDNES.—The annual Christmas tree in connection with the National Sunday Schools took place on Thursday in one of the school-rooms, and there were many visitors during the afternoon and evening. A handsome tree laden with a variety of articles occupied a position in the centre, and there was also a stall. The management of the affair was in the hands of Mesdames Rumfitt, Kilcross, Cave' Crawford, and Davies ; Miss Topham ; Revs. A. P. H. 11 ilson, and C. Rumfitt ; Messrs. Imison and Beattie. A good sum of money had been collected for the occasion by Misses M. Kilcross, G. Balmer, A. Cave, F. Davies. F. Wharton, M. Hughes, L. Edwards, L. Crabtree, L. Neil, Crawford, Pemberton, and Parker. The proceeds will be placed it the disposal of the Vicar to expend as he considers desirable. KILLED IN A QUARRY AT WESTON.—Mr. J. E. Worslev, the deputy coroner, on Tuesday held an inquiry at Weston into the circumstances of the death of George Taylor, aged 57, a labourer who lived at Pritchard's-row, Weston. At twenty minutes to eight on Saturday night, Taylor was seen standing near to Ford's Farm by a woman named Eliza Antrobus. He stated he could not make out his way, and the woman went with him as far as "Snuffy-row." Next morning at ten o'clock his dead body was found at the bottom of N orth-end Quarry by John Johnron, who had been told the deceased had not been home. It was cenjec tured that the deceased had wandered across a field, climbed the fence surrounding the quarry, and fallen, a distance of 50 feet. The deceased's neck was broken, and death must have been iastantaneous. The jury returned a verdict of 'Accidental death," and a hint was thrown out that the proprietors of the quarry might slightly improve the fence. WESLEYAN CONVERSAZIONE AT WIDNES.—The Wesley- ans of Widnes held a conversazione in Lacey-street schools on Saturday with the object of re-imbursing the treasurer for his payments on behalf of the building fund. There was a moderate attendance in the afternoon, when the pro- ceedings were opened by the Rev. R. Burden, in a brief speech. The room had been tastefully decorated for the occasion, and to aid in raising the money two stalls con- taining a variety of articles had been provided. The ladies of the school had stocked one, which was under the control of Mrs Hothersall, Misses Williams and Gillow, and the members of the Band of Hope had been equally generous, the ladies under whose direction the results of their efforts were disposed of being Misses J. Sadler, M. Sadler, Kels all, Poulson, and E. Shadbolt. Theo was also a refreshment stall presided over by Mrs Burden, Mrs B. Brown, Mrs T. Sadler, Misses Abbott, Taylor, Sherratt, and M. J. and E. Sadler. An attractive feature was a Christmas tree, laden with toys, and much interest was centred in a museum of curiosities shown by Mr. Charles Robinson. A capital scientific exhibition was in charge of Messrs. J. Robinson and J. T. Towers. During the evening concerts of an ad- mirable character were given, in which the following took part—Mrs Hothersall, Mrs Richardson, Miss Rowland', Messrs. J. Robinson, J. Shaw, and T. Sherratt. There was also a speaking bee and other amusements. The total pro- ceeds amounted to £3l. It may be mentioned that Meesra. F. Lawrenson and Joseph Robinson were the eecretaries. The proceedings warn continued on Monday evening, when there %veto numerous vi-:i•ors. The total result was t6o. - --- VAGRANCY AT WIDNES.—Yesterday, James Wood and , John McNally were each sentenced to seven days' hard I labour for begging. NON-PAYMENT OF WATER RATES AT RUNCORN. —At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, 50 pe-sons were summoned for the above offence, and the usual orders I were made. I PRINIITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN.—The usual fortnightly meeting was held on Thursday evening in Regent-street Schoolroom. An excellent programme had been drawn up, and a pleasant evening was spent. ANXIOUS TC GO TO GAOL AT RUNCORN.—Yesterday Mary Jane Gallagher, who made her 40th appearance, was charged at Runcorn Police Court with being drunk and dis- orderly. On the previous night Gallagher went to the police office in a state of intoxication and expressed a desire to again visit Knutsford. She refused to leave the office, and at last her conduct was such that Superintendent Leah was obliged to order her " below." She was sentenced to seven days' hard labour and smilingly thanked his wor- ship. WinNns POLICE COURT.—On Thursday James Wood was I fined 78 6d and costs for drunkenness. On the evidence of ' P.S. McGregor and P.C. Tweedle, William Kinclaley was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. Mary Matthews was summoned for assaulting Jane Curley, a married woman, 'living in Viaduct-street. The complainant, whose face bore ' marks of ill-usage, alleged that on Tuesday afternoon the defendant, without any provocation, struck her several times on the face with some weapon and `• blinded her with blood." The defendant accused the complainant of setting a dog at her. The defendant was bound over to keep the i peace three months' or go to gaol 14 days. Dr. Wilkinson. His Lordship has not yet come to a decision.—Manchester Guardian. THE QUEEN'S SPEECH.—The Queen's Speech will be submitted to Parliament on Tuesday, January i I 19th. This date has been fixed n order that mem- bers who are abroad, or at a distance from the I metropolis, may have time to make arrangements to be in their place in the event of a debate aris- ing. Tan MERSEY TUNNEL.—The official inspection of the railway under the Mersey, between Liverpool land Birkenhead, was made on Tuesday by General Hutchinson, on behalf of the Board of Trade. General Hutchinson, who was accompanied by the principal officials of the company, made a thorough inspection of the whole line, and a train was run through the tunnel. It was understood that the re- sult was satisfactory, and that the usual certificate will be granted, SALFORD AND THE SHIP CANAL. At an ad- journed meeting of the Town Council of Salford, on Wednesday. a motion was adopted by a large ma- jority in favour of the promotion in Parliament of ' a bill empowering the Corporation to take shares in the Manchester Ship Canal Company, the money re- quired for the purpose to be borrowed on the security of the rates, revenues, and property of the borough. A poll of the ratepayers will now be taken on the subject. TRA_P ACCIDENT.—On Saturday evening Mr. JO9. Pennington, contractor and builder, Winwick, met with a serious accident whilst driving home about half-past ten. It appears that the horse was going at a good rate, and in turning out of Cross-lane to Crow-lane the trap swerved, and Mr. Pennington was thrown out. He was picked up insensible and carried to the Old Crow Inn, where Dr. Paterson was soon in attendance. On examination Mr. Pen- nington was found to be severely cut and bruised, besides being badly shaken. He is now progress- ing as favourably as can be expected. THE NEW PARLIAMENT.—As at present arranged, Parliajpent will meet on January 12th, and the Queen Speech will be submitted as soon as all the members have been sworn in—probably by Jan. 18th. It is stated that no adjournment will take place between the election of the Speaker, the swearing in of members, and the general business of the House, the latter being entered upon las soon as the House is constituted. The Govern- ment, it is reported, is preparing a bill for removing , the grievances of the crofters of Scotland. The I Duke of Richmond will have charge of the measure, which will be drafted by the Scottish Government departments in Whitehall. A NEw BARONET.—The announcement was made Liverpool, on Wednesday, that Sir Andrew Bar- clay Walker, of Osmaston Manor, Ashbourne, Derby- shire, and Liverpool, had received an intimation that Her Majesty had been pleased to confer upon him a baronetcy. Sir Andrew was in 1877 knighted by the Queen at Windsor Castle, this mark of Royal favour being a recognition of Sir A. B. Walker's munificence in erecting, at a cost of over £40,000, the Liverpool Art Gallery. Since then Sir Andrew has liquidated the cost of the extension of the same building, his total gifts in this direction represent- ing a total of over £70,000. Sir Andrew is a son of the late Mr. Peter Walker, of Auchinflower, Ayr- shire; was born in 1824, and married in 1853 Eliza, , daughter of Mr. John Reid, of Limekilns, Fifeshire, who died in 1882. He is a Conservative, and a jus- tice of the peace for Ayrshire. • THE ILLNESS OF Mn. LATHAM, M.P.—On inquiry 'at Sandbach the other evening, a correspondent WEB informed that there was no improvement in the health of Mr. G. W. Latham, the member for the Crewe division of Cheshire. The hon. gentleman is suffering from rheum:tic gout and an ulcerated i throat, and his condition s such as to cause the greatest anxiety to his friends. The report of his continued prostration has given rise to general re- gret in the Crewe division, which he so gallantly contested and won at the recent election. On Thursday, both the medical attendants—Dr. Lat- ham, of Sandbach, and Dr. Arlidge, of Stoke, had a consultation, and their opinion was unfavourable to the hon. member's ultimate recovery. The news has created intense regret throughout the Crewe division. At ten o'clock on Friday morning there was no improvement in Mr. Latham's condition. CONGREGATIONALISM IN GREAT BRITAIN.—On Thursday the annual returns were issued of the Congregational Churches of Great Britain and Ire- land in the official year book of the Congregational Union of England and Wales. The total number of churches and mission stations associated in England and Wales and returned by the various unions is now 4,218, affording sitting accommodation for 1,555,133 persons. There are also 166 stations re- ported by individual churches, but not included in county returns, thus giving a total of 4,384 places of worship, affording accommodation for 1,582,409 persons. If to these were added the churches in Scotland, Ireland, and the islands of the British seas, there are about 4,600 places of worship in Great Britain belonging to the Congregational body. There are also nearly 700 churches in the British colonies, Australia being first with 334 churches, and Canada next with 168. Lancashire returns 291 churches, with accommodation for 142,007 persons; and Yorkshire 304 churches, with accommodation for 154,163. In Cheshire there are 73 churches, which provide 29,081 sittings. ALEXANDRA THEATRE, LIVERPOOL.—The panto- mime .of "Cinderella" at the Alexandra Theatre, Liverpool, has become a success of the most extra- ordinary character, and has greatly enhanced the ' previously high reputation of the theatre and of Mrs. Saker and the whole of her staff. The magni- ficent scenery has been the theme of universal praise, and the many delightful episodes of the pan- tomime are so varied and beautiful that many who have already seen the pantomime under the incon- venient circumstances of crowded houses are deter- mined to go again to enjoy the wonderful spectacles that are presented. The acting of the various char- acters has become more full of genuine humour and pantomimic business, and the specialities that are introducted—such as the flying lady, .2Enea ; the pigeon charmer, Mdlle. Garetta ; the real hounds and the hunting scene are provocative of un- bounded admiration and wonderment. Another feature of the show which recalls the best days of artistic ballet is the charming dancing of Mcllle. Petoldi. , The superb transformation scene of Mr. Brunton is the climax of a series of artistic displays that have never previously been equalled on the local stage. On Monday the Alexandra Theatre was crowded to its utmost limit both morning and evening.

MYSTERIOUS FATALITY ON RUNCORN BRIDGII.

About half-past seven on Thursday morning, the muti- lated body of a man was found on the London and North- Western Railway on the Widnes side of Runcorn Bridge. The body was lying in the "four-foot" of the down line, and the head, which was completely severed, was in the "six-foot." Sergeant Robinson had the remains conveyed to the Bridge Hotel, Widnes, where he searched the cloth- ing. Papers were found showing that the unfortunate man was Martin Kaley, fireman on a steamer. Besi lee seven seamen's. discharges bearing this name, there was a .letter dated December 2nd from 45, High-street, Canningtown, 'London, E.. and signed Catherine Kaley, and other articles. In an empty compartment of the last train from Lime-street there was discovered on its arrival at Runcorn a parcel containing a shirt and a pair of shoes. A clue to the acci- dent was found in the man's waistcoat pocket. This was a ticket from Lime-street to A..erton, and it is supposed that finding he had been over-carried, the deceased jumped from the carriage, and was killed by a passing train.

div.head: CHILD SUFFOCATED AT WIDNES. PARENTAL NEGLECT.
div.p: A CHILD SUFFOCATED AT WIDNES. PARENTAL NEGLECT.

Mr. W. T. Husband, tke deputy coroner, on Wednesday held an inquiry at the George Hotel, vl idnes, touching the death of the infant daughter of Thomas Urine, a labourer, who lives at 3, Milton-street. The evidence showed that on Sunday night the parents retired to rest about half-past ten. and the child, according to the mother, against the wall, and according to the father, in the centre of the bed. Next morning at a quarter to eight the mother arose and went down stairs to perform her household duties. The infant. which was nina weeks old, was then apparently all right. The husband had his breakfast in bed, and then got up and went to the kitchen without looking at the child. At hay- past eight the mother found it lying on the bed dead. One side of its body was black. The husband admitted that when he went to bed he bad had three pints of beer, but he wasnot drunk.—The Deputy Coroner said this appeared to be one of those preventible accidents which were so com- mon, and which could be easily avoided by the least fore- thought and care. There had been gross negligence on the part of the parents, but he did not think it had been inten- tional. If the jury thought this man was drunk when he went to bed, and was suffering from the effects in the morning, or was too ill to pay much attention to the child by his side, this would be culpable negligence to say the least, and he would deserve the severest censure. The Deputy Coroner pointed out, however, that at the Assizes these cases were looked upon as purely accidental, and a convic- tion had not vet been recorded, and he would not advise a committal. He referred in strong terms to the man's lazi- ness in getting his breakfast in bed and without taking the trouble to look at the infant, which was warm when found dead, and had doubtless died after the mother had arisen.— The jury, after some minutes consideration, brought in a verdict that the child was accidently suffocated, and added that the father ought to be severely reprimanded. Grice was then called into the room, and received a severe lecture from the Deputy Coroner on his careless conduct. His fee for attending as a witness was also stopped.

div.head: PAYMENT OF JURYMEN AT WIDNES.
div.p: THE PAYMENT OF JURYMEN AT WIDNES.

At the conclusion ef an inquest at the George Hotel, Widnek On Wednesday, Joseph j.3.111W02, ; lair, referred to the subject of the payment of jurymen. Widnes trades- men, he said, thought it a great hardship that they should be taken away from their business so frequently, and receive no remuneration for their services.—Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, said be thought with the jury, that they ought to be paid for their services; but the custom of the eountry was that a man should serve his Queen and COUR- *try for nothing. These ancient notions were, however, gradually dying out, and there was no doubt the time would come when jurymen would be paid like other persons who rendered services to the Crown or to their town. At present there was no means of giving jurymen fees unless they arranged the matter themselves. It was for them to start, and he would help them all he could. They had got a member of Parliament, and be had no doubt if they asked him nicely he would do his utmost to have the law altered to enable jurymen to obtain teem. But he did not think Parliament would take esp this subj.ct at preuent. He was of opinion, however, that if they called an, influential meeting of the town.people that the Local Board would collect a voluntary rate sufficient to pay jurymen on inquests 2s 6d, and these who attended the assizes 5s per day.—A Juryman Is it usual to pay jurymen ?—The Deputy Coroner replied that it was usual in many places. In Garston jurymen rec.ived half a crown. Many wealthy people lived in Gorgon who preferred to pay a farthing in the pound rather than attend on a jury, and there were many trrdesmen who would rather attend upon an inquest and receive half a crown than 'not get it.—Mr. Brookes: But those gentlemen who pay the farthing in the pound are not exempt at all.—The Deputy Coroner: No, they are not exempt.—Another Juryman: I think 99 out of every 100 jurymen are taken either from the shopkeepers or publicans. This jury is composed entirely of these class.F, and I think it is a great hardship.—The Deputy Coroner said if they would apply to Mr. Brighouse, and appoint a committee, they could find out how many persons had served upon juries during the past three years. There were doubtless many people who had not nerved on juries —The jury then departed. NEW YEAR'S FESITVITIRS AT RUNCORN AND

FOOTBALL MATCH AT WlDNES.—Yesterday, the first team of the Runcorn Recreation Club met Widnes vcond fifteen on the hatters ground at Moorhouse-lane. Much in- terest was centred in the game, and the five hundre., spec- tators that assembled had a pleasing and skilful exhibition of football. Neither team was at its Intl strength, hut the game was very equelly contested, and during the first half only a minor point was scored to the credit of Widnes. In the second half Widnes added a try, obtained by Penning- ton, from a splendid pass by Wright, and a minor. The Recreation made no ',core. For Widnes, Pennington, Howard, and Wr iglit e,ere the pick of the backs, and Bing- ham, Wright, and McGuri played we!l up in the forwards. Whinyates played a epiendid game for the Recreation, and Charlestown was very safe at. lull back. Fox, Acton, and Bate were prominent amongst the forwards. BAPTIST BAZAAR AT WIDNES —Yesterday, New Year's Day, a sale of work was held in the Baptist Chep-I, Nelsen- street, in aid of the fund for building a new chapel. The Interior of the structure had been made bright by holly and bancerettee, and on each side of the morn was a stall crowded with articles, the product of the self-sacrificing labours of the ladies of the sewing meeting and nuneerous kind friend. There was also a refreshment stall and a Christmas tree laden with "fruit " of a seasonable charec- ter. The verions amusements of a heater were provided, including an electric battery and an exhibition of curiosities, The fair saleswomen were Misses Thompson, Seddon, Bailey, Rate life, Passey, Wood, Mackereth, Welling, Davies, Moores, Priestnall. The Rev. R Yee!. man, the pastor, conclacted the proceedings at the opening ceremony. In his address he remarked that they desired a new chapel not bec ruse the present building was crowded. As a rule the congregations were very good, but they were subjected to incidents of a very disagreeable character. They could hardly have a meetiniz 1 on a week day or a Sunday without annoyance from hove ' and youths in the locality, and another great reason for removal to a better locality was the fact that they were in the midst of the works, and subjected to smoke and gases of a most disagreeable nature. During the past two years there had been an increase of 20 members, And an improvement in almost every other direction, but thy had not made that headway and progress that the earnest labours of the mem- bers should have. When be undertook the pastorate two years ago only £l3 had been obtained towards the fund for ilae erection of a new chapel. They had now £l7B in the bank. mostly obtained withont outside help. Mr. R B. Davies bad promised £5. Mr. Vickers £5. Mr. T. Snape £l, and Mr. Meunsey, who was unable to be present, hail for- warded a cheque for £l.—Mr. J. Cripps, of Wa'erloo Park, Liverpool, then ppforrned the epening ceremony in a neat speech, expressing hie interest in the work in which the Baptist denomination were engaged in Wir:nee.—He was cordially thanked on the motion of Mr. E. Carey, seconded by Mr. W. Clarke.—Mr. Yeetman announced that that afternoon Mr. Cripps had given him a donation of £5, and Mr. Carey a donation of £2. (Applause.)—The sale then , commenced.

FOUND DROWNED IN THE MERSEY. Yesterday morning a labourer, who was engaged in the alteration of a weir near the Old Warps, War- rington, in the river Mersey, discovered the body of a man, which was in such a decomposed state as to be almost unrecognisable. The body was clothed in a dark rough tweed suit and strong lace-up boots, with thick iron tips. It had evidently been in the water a long time. In one of the pockets of the trousers of the deceased was found a knife and 7s 7d in money. The police were communicated with, and from the clothing of the deceased it was surmised that it was possible that the body might be that of an Irish labourer who disappeared very suddenly some time back. It will be remembered that a fight took place between some Irish labourers on Friars' Green late on a Saturday evening, and that one of the men went away in the direction of the river, and was not heard of again. One of the labourers engaged in the row was subsequently ar- rested by the borough police, and charged before the magistrates on suspicion of murdering his com- panion, but as no evidence could be produced to show what had become of that companion, or to ac- tually prove that he was dead, the accused was 'discharged on undertaking to appear if called upon. ' Acting on the supposition that the body found might be that of the missing man, a member of the borough force yesterday proceeded to Altrincham, in the neighbourhood of which place the parties in question lived, to see if anything could he learned , with a view to identification.

div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.

1886 was ushered in in a similar manner at the twin towns at the Mersey. At both place. well attended watch- night services were held in the churches of the Establish- ment and in the Nonconformist chapels, sermons appropri- ate to the occasion being preached. Tbe weather, though damp and heavy, was very mild, and the streets bore an aspect of animation, which increased as the church bells rang forth merry peals, and the "buzzers" of the works sent forth hearse cries of greetirg to the new year. Wai's and bands of music made sounds melodious, but groups of young men and youths took advantage of the occasion to make " night hideous" by diecordant sboutings and the misuse of wind instruments. Amongst the events that took place was a TRADESMEN'S BALL AT Wiprews.—This was held at the Baths, Victoria-road, on New Year's Eve, and was well patronised. Mr. T. Swinton officiated as M.C., and dancing was indulged in until an early hour to the strains of a string band conducted by Mr. J. Gordon.

GOOD TEMPLARISM AT WIDNES.—Last night a tea party was held in connection wits the Haste to the Rescue Lodge 1.0.G.T. at the Science Buildings. Major Cross-street. There was a good attendance, and Sisters M. Kirkham, Galilee, Smith, and Griffiths presided at the tables. Subse- coently an entertainment took place. There were singing and recitation contests by the members of the John Wesley Juvenile Temple, which meets at Moss Bank. Then the members of Haste to the Rescue Lodge went through an admirable programme of songs, recitations, and dialogues. FOOTBALL Jenkins, andiiii A JohnTcß AR T Robinson. o Speeches were delivered by Brothers Griffiths, Henry Smith, R. RN.—A large concourse ef spectators assembled on Runcorn Football Field yesterday afternoon, to witness a match between Rochdale St. Clement's and the home first fifteen. By means of a little luck the visitors scored a try before play had been in pro- gress five minutes. The kick at goal failed, and Runcorn assuming the aggressive, gave their opponents same work, Speakman equalising matters by a splendid try, which Woe is failed to convert into the premier point. Daring the second half play was chiefly in the visitors quarters, and their lines were crossed three times. The ball was, however, ruled back on each occasion' and a good drop goal by Broady met a similar fate. The game ended in a draw in favour of Runcorn by 1 try and 6 minor points to 1 try and two minor points. The teams were as follow :—St. Clements—Back, Monlsworth ; three-quarter backs, Rigg, Pratt. and Collinge ; half backs, Richardson and Kenyon; Rigg, Holt, McHugh, Ashworth, Ridehaugh, Clegg, Johnson, S. Holt, Hampson. Runcorn—Back, Woods; three-quarter backs, Speakman, Johnson, Wain. wright ; half backs, Hughes and Andrews; W. Wright, Broady, Hughes, Lewis, Hoffiand, Barns, Joule, Gatley, Clarke. TREAT TO NEWS BOYS AT Witorres.—Last evening the whole of the news boys who sell the daily and weekly papers, without distinction, in Widnes and the district, were entertained at a splendid tea by Mrs. and Miss Morewood in the large room at Mr. Thomas Edwardson's Mineral Waters Manufactory, Hibbertestreet, Widnes. The treat, which was the best of the kind ever given in the town, was con- tributed to by the Rev. George Bond, vicar of Farnworth ; the Rev. James Clark, P.P., Lngsdale; Mr. T. C. Edwards. Moe', M.P.; Dr. Booth, and other local gentlemen. the room was tastefully decorated with mottoes and other seasonable ornamentations kindly given by Mrs. Edwards, news agent. Simms Cross; the tables and forms were lent by the trustees of the Malins Temperance Hall ; and tbe earthenware by Mrs Hurst, general dealer, Widnes-road. After tea, at which there were over 50 boys present, games of various descriptions were indulged in, and a very plea- sant and profitable period was devoted to singing, recita- tions, and other innocent amusements. Previous to the party breaking up, hearty votes of thanks were passed to the various donors, the compliments in each case being moved and seconded by the boys themselves, some of whom made very intelligent speeches and gave expression to their sentiments in a very creditable manner. MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN.—The annual tea meeting in connection with the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen was held on New Year's Eve, at Bottom Locks. There was a good attendance, and the tables were presided over by Mrs Meadowcroft, Mrs H. Abel, Mra Hodgson, Mrs Allen, and Mrs R. Hnlmes. Subsequently a public meeting and entertainment took place under the presidency of Mr. J. Meidowcroft. le a brief speech the chairman referred to the admirable work the mission was accomplishing amongst the boatmen and seamen, and mentioned that the children who attended the Sunday School were so numerous that the present building was not sufficiently large. The following programme was gone through in good style :—Recitation, "Faith in God," Ada Handle ; song, Miss Crosby ; recitation, "Bonny brid," Master Tom Saunders; song, Mr. Jones ; recitation, "A ghost story," Miss B. Holland ; song, Mr. Joule ; reading, Mr. Hodgson ; song, Miss Crosby ; song, " Bessie," Ada Randle' recitation," Somebody's mother," J. W.. Holt ; sang, Mr. E. Hobson : recitation, Herbort Hedgcock ; clerionet solo, Mr. Jones ; recitation, Martha Hon ind. Mr. George Howard was the accompanist. The usual votes of thanks having been accorded, the remainder of the eveniug was spent in social games.

DEATH OF Mus. Howsoiv.—A. most painful sensation was caused at Chester, on Wednesday morning, by the untimely death, following so close upon that of her husb ind, of Mrs. Howson, at the Deanery. A short time since in walking to the front gate a servant trod upon Mrs. Howson's dress and she fell, fracturing her leg. ISuffering from a serious and, as afterwards proved, a fatal illness, Dean Howson went to Bournemouth, and thither Mrs. Howson, despite great cut- feting from her fractured leg, followed, and nursed him to the end. After the death of her husband she returned to Chester, took to her bed, and died at four o'clock on Wed- nesday morning. The keenest sorrow is felt at Chester for the children bereaved of father and mother within a few days. The Home Secretary has given the Cathedral autho- ritiea of Chester permission to inter the remains of Mrs. Howson in the grave of the late Dean, situate in the cloister green of the Cathedral. The interment will take place ta- *lay (Saturday). MURDERS AND ATTEMPTED MURDERS.—John HEVeq, a mark maker, at Sheffield, Stabbed his wife on Saturday night with a large pocket knife, and afterwards severed his Own windpipe. The woman is expected to recover, but the man is in a dangerous state.—James Whitehall, a ,j9anner, living at 5, Drury-lane, London, quarrelled with his wife on Saturday afternoan, attacked her with a pen- knife, and inflicted -a superficial cut extending from the left ear to the middle of her throat. She ran screamin4 down the stairs and escaped. Whitehall was found lying on. the floor with his throat terribly cut. The knife found ly.ing by his side had cut deeply through the throat. He died in a few minutes —Bernhardt Vogt, a German stonemason, was charged at Bow-street, London, on Satur- day, upon an extradition warrant, with having murdered gamekeeper named Krake, at Willebadessen, in Germany. Sir J. Ingham stated that the papers relating to the case had not yet reached him, and remanded the prisoner.--At Chesterfield, on Momlay, Edward Hass, a man alaioet was renaandFd en the charge of killing Thomas Evans, his lodger. It is alleged that on Saturday night the prisoner attacked. Evans with a poker. and, having knocked him down, kicked him in the stomach. Evans, woo was a weakly man, got up. apparently not much the worse for hi. ill-treatment, but died on Monday morning in the prisoner', house. '

CHRISTMAS AND NEW YEAR'S
FESTIVITIES.

In Warrington there was little in the outward show to distinguish New Years's Day from any or- dinary week day. In the morning the shops and various places of business seemed almost without exception to be opened in the accustomed way, and to judge from the appearance of the streets the workmen of the town appeared to be for the most part engaged in their usual avocation. In the after- noon, however, a number of shops, the banks of the town, and several other places of business were closed, and in the evening a number of gatherings of a more or less public character were held. On New Year's Eve, towards midnight, the streets were pretty well frequented, and at many of the churches and chapels, including St. Pauls Church, Holy Trinity Church, Wycliffe Congregational Church, and Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel, watch-night services were held. The weather both on New Year's Eve and yesterday was certainly not of the kind that is considered "seasonable," being remtukably mild and spring-like, and the roads and paths instead of being hard bound in frost, were muddy and slippery. lesterday afternoon, the only event of a public character was a football match between teams of the Warrington and Bootle football clubs, which was well attended, and resulted in an easy victory for the home players by 2 goals, 8 tries, and 1 minor point to nil. Below we give accounts of the more important fes- tivities which have taken place. Sr. PAUL'S INFANT SCHOOL—The %nnual tea, pary in connection with this school took plAce in the scnoultoom yesterday afternoon, when the children had a bea•ty repast. The Rev. S. Wi'ltinson (pastor) and a number of gentlemen who identify themselves with the work of the geh..l were present, and ma ie very successful efforts to amuse the young ones.

GRAPPENHALL PARISH CHIIRCH.—The annual tea party in connection with this church was held in the larde room at Grappenhall, on Thursday. There was a good number present. Subsiquently Mr. Walter Roselle, of Liverpool, gave an entertainment entit:ed "Flashes of fun," which was listened to with much pleasure, some parts of it being provocative of touch laughter. TEA PARTY AT Cliorr.—A tea party WAS held at the Joiners' Arms Inn, at the above place on Saturday evening, upwards of 50 persons being present. Dancing was after- wards engaged in until closing time. Songs, &c, were given by Mr. and Mrs Lewis Battersby, of Kenyon, Mr. William Battersby, of Culchetb, and others. Mr. W. Bat- terslT accompanied on the piano.

VOLUNTEER BALL.—Tne annual New Year's ball in con- nection with the Warrington corps of the Ninth Lancashire Rifle Volunteers was held in the Drill Shed on Thursday evening, when there was a large attendance. Music was provided by the band of the corps, and dancing was kept up with spirit until the early hours of the New Year. Refresh- ments were supplied by Mr. Warburton, of the Old Crow. Bridge-street. THE SILVER-STREET MISSION.—On Saturday evening a free tea was provided in the Silver-street Wesleyan Schoolroom for the poor people living in the neighbour- hood of Silver-street. The treat was given in connection with the Silver-street Gospel Temperance Mission and Band of Hope, which is doing good work, and, needless to say, was greatly appreciated. A large number of poor people enjoyed the good things provided, which were ex- cellent and plentiful, and which were dispensed by naanv willing bands. Oranges, itc., were also given away.

WeitnisoroN BUIE COAT SCHOOL.--An excellent tea and supper were given by Lady Oreenall on Wedneedav evening to the pupils of the Blue Coat School. The tea, consisting of currant and seed bread, buns, tt.c., was served at five o'clock, and was presided over by Mr and Mrs Rose. The room had been very tastefully decorated for the occa- sion with evergreens and suitable mottoes. During the evening nuts and gingerbread were freely distributed, and the children amused themselves with various games. A hearty supper ef pork pies and coffee having been partaken of, cheers were given for Sir Gilbert and Lady Cireenall, ad the children retired to rest at nine o'clock, haying spent every pleasant evening. THE WORKHOUSE.—At the Workhouse prizes which had been subscribed for by friends of the inmates were distribu- ted yesterday evening to over 100 children and some of the harmless imbeciles. The prizs were hung on a Christmas tree which bad beim preseeted by Mr. John White, and were taken off and given to each of the children in their turn, the gifts evidently being very much appreciated by the juve- niles. Afterwards a musical entertainment was given, several songs, &c., being given by ladies and gentlemen who had kindly volunteered their services. Altogether a very pleasant evening was spent, the children and other inmates heartily enjoying themselves under the careful superinten- dence of the Master and Matron, Mr. and Mrs. Mackay._

TEA PARTY AT THE CROFT BOARD SCHOOLS.—The chtft of Christ Church, Croft, and the members of the village drum and fife band, to the number of upwards of 59, were entertained to tea on Saturday evening by the Rev. T. P. and Mrs. Kirkman After tea, dancing and various games were indulged in until ten o'clock, when the company were supplied with cogee, buns, c. Miss Kirkman supplied the music for dancing. The following songs were creditably given during the evening, Mr. Ball accompanying on the harmonium :—"Venetian boat song," Mr. J. H. Waywell ; part song. "The evening lullaby," choir; song, "God pro- tect England," Mr. George Clough; song, "If I'm poor, I'm a gentleman still," Mr. Joseph Sylvester; song, " Untasted sweets," Miss Annie %tines. The proceedings were brought to a close shortly after ten o'clock, after the National An- them had been sung and th.nks given to the rector and Mrs. and Miss Kirkman for their kindness.

BANK QUAY MISSION.—The annual gathering of the scholars and teachers of the Sunday school connected with Bank Quay Mission took place on Monday evening, and was a decided success. A substantial tea was partaken of. and subsequently Mr. John Crosfield, J.P.. presided at a crowded meeting of parents and acbolars. After a hymn had been sung and prayer offered up. Mr. W. Ford, secre- tary, read the annual report of the work of the school dur- ing the last twelve months, which was received with ap- plause, the school being in a very flourishing condition.— Tine Chairman said that he had listened with great interest to the excellent report,which was a credit to the Secretar7 and to the school. He was glad to hear that the school was in a flourishing condition, and he was led to think that when be built that place as a Sunday School there was no place about that end of the town for the parents to send their children, and now they saw that since the mission was built there was a church school, Sankey Bridges, and St. Barnabas schools, which, he had no doubt, were very well attended. He would remind the children and also the parents that they were much indebted to the teachers for their service., and hoped they would send their children on Sunday mornings, He wished the all A Happy New Year." (Applause.) The following are the officers for the ensuing year, viz., Messrs. Williamson and Hough, super- intendents; W. Ford, secretary; J. Dawber, treasurer; Joseph Monks, senr. visitor.—At the close of the meeting Mr. Dale moved a vete of thanks to the Chaiman. Mr. George Dale seconded, and Mr. R. Williamson ably sup- ported it. Mi. Crosfield, after suitably replying, received quite an ovation as he passed throu,:;l2 the room, accom- panied by Miss Dixon and Miss Crosfield, who had occupied seats en the platform. The following programme was very creditably gone through in the course of the evening, viz. : —Chorus by Choir, Ringing cheerily ;" recitation, Willie Tornkinson ; recitation, Miss Fanny Ashton; song, "Tread softly the angels are calling," Mrs. David Monks; address, Mr. George Dale; chorus, "Christmas bells," Choir ; re- citation, John Middleton; recitation, Mary Ellen Tomkin- son; recitation, "Selected," Mr. David Monks; song, " Almost persuaded," Mr. D. Dunn; recitation. "Jack and Jill," Alice Thomas; recitation, Ellen Humphries ; chorus, "Stand like men," seven children ; this latter piece being sung a second time at the request of Mr. Crosfield.

SANKEY BRIDGES W ESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. —Oll Saturday the ninth annual meeting was held in connection with the above Sunday School, when a substantial tea was provided, including beef and ham sandwiches. The pro- gramme of the evening was an interesting one, commencing *ith a sale of surplus stock of goods left at the recent bazaar for chapel building funds. The goods to be sold having been previously made known by circular, a large number of friends assemb:ed, and the sale, conducted by Mr. Summers- gill, was very lively and spirited, the whole of the stock being rapidly disposed of. The Rey. J. McTurk afterwards took the chair and gave a humourous and instructive ad- dress. Mr. A. George, secretary of the school, also made his report, which showed that the schools were in a healthy condition. The finances were given by Mr. Summersgill, who also spoke of the pleasure he took in the cause of God. and his desire for its prosperity.* He likewise referred to the need of giving more light to some portions of the new chapel and doing away with the cold draft tt, in- conveniences many of the seat holders, and also the ne city of matting the aisle walks in the chapel.—Mr. J. s. Sncddy addressed the meeting on the advantage to Sunday school teachers of constancy and perseverance in their work, and the value of Bands of Hope.—Mr. R. Lawton, visitor of absentees, spoke on the many difficulties caused by drink the children had to contend with, and gave some instances that bad come under his own observation.—Mr. S. Blythe spoke upon his attachment to the Sunday school, and par- ticularly to his class, and drew attention to the preveiling drunkenneee among females, and especially among young women. He expressed hie fear lest the new Parliament should neglect legislation for its suppression, and spoke of the need of an earnest study of God's word, and of correct views of doctiine, and also of geography, &c.—Mr. T. Wooley gave an encouraging speech dwelling upon the healthy condition of the school, and the fact that several scholars had joined the church Mr. B. Walker referred to the love that he had for his work AS a teacher, and his purpose to gain their cenfidence;and of 1 the importance of young people beingled to the forming of good habits.—Mr. W. Pacey, of the Men's Bible Class, spoke of its advantages and blessings to himself, and urged the need of diligent earnest work in their cottage services.— Mr. J. Hardy gate similar testimony as to the benefits 'derived from his connection with the Men's Bible Class.— Mr. F. Braithwaite spoke upon the desirability of looking , well to the children on week days as we'l as on Sundays, and to study the disposition of each child in their classee. and of itspeeeeitag tie children with the fact that true re-

ligion is a joyous thing.—lt may be mentioned that tilt ladies who presided at the tea tables were Mrs. Summersgill, Mrs. Hough, Mrs. Blythe, Mrs. Walker, Mn. Williamson, Mrs. Tonge, Mrs. Ogden, Mrs. Pacey, rnd the Misses Sum- mersgill, Dunn, Tonge, and Walker. A cordial vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close. On Monday, the children's tea party was held, the room being crowded. After tea games were freely indulged in, a merry meeting being brought to a close about half-past nine. It may be added that the number of boys attending this school is 118, and of girls 105 ; the member admitted this year is 42, left 9, the increase for the year consequently being 33. The average attendance:is—morning 92, afternoon 183. There are 32 church members, the increase this year being 12. The following are the officers and teachers, viz.: —Superintendents, Messrs. Summersgill, George, and Snoddy ; secretary, Mr. A. George; treasurer, Mr. W. Sum- tnerfield ; visitor, Mr. R. Lawton ; teachers, Mrs. Braitb. waite, Mrs. Pacey, Miss Summersgill, and Miss Walker. and Messrs. S. Blythe, Corydine, J. Hough, T. Whalley, F. Braithwaite, W. Brough, H. Ogden, B. Walker, C. Prit- chard, W. Tonokinson, S. Schofield, and C. George. A solemn and deeply interesting watch-night service was held in Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel on New Year's Ere, commencing about half-past ten o'clock. There was a good attendance. Mr. Summersgill conducted the service, and Mr. Tomkinson preaided at the harmonium. At mid. night the congregation engaged in silent prayer, after which the appropriete hymn "Come let us anew cur journey pursue," was sung. A final prayer having been engaged in. the company dispersed, heartily wishing each other "A happy new year." CONGRATULATIONS AT THE COUNTY COURT. On the conclusion of the buslness for the day at the County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffeulkes rose from his seat, Mr. P. Davies. solicitor, War- rinetonon behalf of himself and tbe other advocates present, wished his Honour a happy New Year. His Honour, in reply, said that he was very much obliged, and he hoped that the wish would be fulfilled. The year had ended with rather a heavy cloud upon it to him, owing to the unusual number of deaths of personal friends of his own that had taken place within the lastifew we-ks. He hoped that the new year would be better in its inception than the old was in its closing. In return he heartily wished all a happy new year. His Honour then rcse, and the suhject droppea.

div.head: HILL CLIFFE BAPTIST CHURCH.
div.p: HILL CLIFFE BAPTIST CHURCH.

A pamphlet just issued contains an interesting account of the ancient Baptist Church at Hill Cliffe, near Warrington. The writer, after giving a general sketch treating on the early introduction of Christianity into England, speaks specially of Hill Cliffe as a place of meeting for Christian worship- pers at an early date, and that it was so, because the great object in view was concealment from the persecutors of the early Christian Church, many of whom, he states, were Baptists, although not then known by that name. Hill Cliffe until recent times was surrounded by woods, and at a safe distance from public highways, and being very near the boundaries of the counties of Lancashire and Ches- hire, it was permanently safe, and it was an easy matter when persecutions were strong in Cheshire to remove into Warrington, where there was a meet- ing house in connection with Hill Cliffe Chapel. The references to Hill Cliffe burial ground date to 1337; but it is 200 years after that before any re- cords are found showing the existence of the place of worship. There are various gravestones dating as far back as 1513 and 1599. Various extracts are given from works treating on the subject of ancient churches in this and adjoining neighbourhoods which make the pamphlet particularly interesting. It appears that in 1710 the first Baptist Church at Liverpool was formed, and was known as a distinct Baptist church by the mother church at Hill Cliffe. Mr. Turner was the minister at Hill Cliffe in 1714, and it appears from ancient documents that he received contributions from " Liverpoole," Ches- ter, '`Namptwich," &c. Mr. Turner remained in the ministry until 1727. From 1740 until 1759 the well-known Dr. MacGowan, author of 6' Dialogues of Devils," was minister, carrying on the trade of a bread baker in Bridge-street, Warrington, at the same time. In 1839 the Rev. A. Kenworthy became the pastor, and remained so until 1876. He is still living in the neighbourhood, and takes an active part in local ministerial and general public work. On his retirement he had a massive gold watch and chain and an easy chair and writing desk presented to him..

div.p: BELVSEY•ROAD WW-LEYAN CHAPEL.

The second of a furies of ternperat a• services was btl I in Bewsey-road Wesleran Chapel on Thursday evening. when the chair was occupied by the Rev G. B. Cutting. Tlfre was a good attendance. Several speeches were made which took the form of testimony, and many who had been alikc- ted to drink a• one time related how they bad been induced to abandon the growing habit. Mr. John Bennett, jun., of Leeds, made a stirring address, advecating the cause of tem- perance in a forcible manner. Sergeants Gilbert and Prag- nall, from Orford barracks, also spoke. Short speeches were given by men of many ranks and csnditions, but all agreed in expressing thankfulness that they had cliscon- tinucd drinking habits. During the evening several per- sons, principally young men, responded to an invitation to take the pledge. Hymns were sung by the choir, aCCDal- panieti on the organ by 4,r. James. On the conclusion of the Band of Hope meetiO a coffee supper was partaken of in the large vestry, at which a good number sat down. A watcbnight service, conducted by the Rev. G. E. Cutting. followed. Mr. Cutting was assisted by Mr. Green, Mr. He,- ' wocd, and others. WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.

Servit was held in this church on Thursday evening, commencing at 11-15. A hymn was sung, and the Rev. John Yorge then read a portion of Scripture. Afterwards those present were addressed by the Rev. John Yonge, who spoke of the year past and the lessons to be derived from it for future guidance, expressing a hope that they would make better use of the coming year than they had done of the past. Twelve months ago, he said, a similar service was held, at which he used the words "lime is short," and pointed out that in the revised version the words were "'rime is shortened." He then spoke of it being shortened for the purpose of working out their salvation. Their time for that purpose was shorter still that night. Some people !coking back on the year 1885, seemed to think that in some respects it was a very dull one. Dullness usually had the characteristic of slowness, but he thought they must have signs to look back upon to show them that every Year they lived seemed to go more quickly than the :,ear that preceded it. Services like that were intended for the pur- pose of helping them to reflect upon the past, and seemed to come to them as a pause amid the rush and hurry and haste of life—a pause in order that they might look back on the past, and look forward with a resolution for re better and holier life. They would agree with him that it would be a sad and terrible thing for any of them to say that life had not attained for them its real purposes. Why were they put into this world ? Was man's life simply what they might term an accident, or was there a separate, a die. tinct, and a definite purpose for which God had made us ? He thought that when they looked back upon their lives they would readily admit that there was a purpose, and a great reason why we had been made and kept in being. Some people seemed to regard life merely as an opportunity for the enjoyment of temporal pleasures, and to secure to themselves as much as they could of this world's goods, profits, and pleasures. Of the great multitude there were some who gained a tolerable amount of the profits and plea- sures of the world, but by tar the greater number of the multitude of men got very little profit and pleasure out of this earthly world. But if they considered they would learn that this was not God's purpose, and that His purpose and idea was that they should prepare fer the grand, glorious, and divine future. He looked upon this life as a kind of school, where God was the educator. In conclusion he urged them not to centre their thoughts alone on earthly matters, but to think well of the future. CONVERSAZIONE AT PENKRTH.

The annual conversazione ha connection with Penketh Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society—which numbers about one hundred members and holds very successful weekly meetings—was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, , Penketh, on Wednesday evening. Although the weather was wet and windy there were a large number of visitors present. The building had been prettily decorated. Ap- propriate mottoes, trimmed with evergreens, were fixed on the walls at the sides and ends of the room, and pictures were interspersed. Decorations of evergreens hung pendant from the ceiling, and additional light was provided by large Chinese lanterns suspended from the ceiling and underneath the evergreens. Amongst those present were Mr. Charles Parker, president of the society, Miss Parker, Mr. and Mrs. R. Garnett, and the Misses Garnett, Mrs Gornall, Mr. David Garnett, Mr. Brett, Mr. and Mrs. Mainley, Mr. and Mrs. Randall, Mr. and Mrs. Watson, Mr. T. H. Wilson I(secretary of the society), and Mrs Wilson, the Miqses Routledge, Mr. and Mrs T. Seed, Dr. Harter, Mr. E. Cross, Mr. B. Hobson, Mr. and Mrs. John Atherton, Mr. and Mrs. Cross, &c., tc. The decorations were tinder taken by Messrs. White, Moores, and Hobson, and bY Miss Garnett, Misses Ellen and Fanny Garnett, and the 'Misses Moses. Several of the ladies presided over a well-stocked refreshment stall On tables placed round the room various curiosities were exhibited. Mr. Henry Burns, of Liverpool, exhibited a number of ants, and during the evening gave a short treatise on ants in their nests. The ants were viewed through microscopes and formed an interesting study. In some of the cases several Queen ants were living amicably together, and in one the ants were shown with their atten- dant slaves. Another exhibit comprised two keys made by inmates of the Yorkshire County Asylum for the purpose of effecting an escape; one of the keys had been manufactured from a piece of bone and the other from a nail. There were also on eihibition a cavalry sword carried through the Indian Mutiny by the late Robert Allen, of Penketh; a Russian pen case and ink bottle found on the field of battle after the fall of Sebastopol ; a case of leaves from Colorado, &c.; a number of Bibles in different lan- guages, lent ley Dr. Mackie; and samples of dyes taken from different kind of wood and bark. There was also a collection of birds' eggs and butterflies collected by Miss Garnett, of Hall Nook, in the summers of 1883-4. Mr. Madelev, of the Warrington Museum, exhibited two slow-worms, which were placed in a small box, and were the recipients of mach curiosity. An interesting feature of the evening's enioy- ment was a scientific explanation of the functions of the air pump, given by Dr. Hurter. After the visitors had in- spected the articles on view. the President (Mr. Parker) ad- dressed a few words to them, remarking that be hoped that all would make themselves at home and enjoy themselves thoroughly; the best way to accomplish that was to determine to farther the enjoyment of ethers. Afterwards the followirg programme was efficiently rendered : Pianoforte duet, "Caller Herrin," Misses N and F Garnett ; flute solo, Mr W Johnson; duet, "We two," Miss Garnett and Mr R E Garnett; trio, "La Serenata," Miss A Moses. Miss F Garnett, and Mr S W Fades (violin) ; song, Mr. P. Johnston, "Toni Bowling"; duet, "The Ash Grove," Mrs Wilson and Mr Watson; violin solo, Mr S W Fildes; reci- tation, "The "Legend of Lochbuy," Mr R E Garnett; double quartett, "Farewell," Misses L and F Garnett, Misses J and A Moses, Messrs P Johnson and R E Garnett, I Messrs D Garnett and J Watson.

nuaDißors ENCOUNTER WITH A BURGLAR IN Mar 4 caEsTEn..—At Manchester City Police-court, on Tuesday, John Carragon was charged with breaking into the Friend- ship Tavern, Buckley-street, and murderously assaulting the landlord. About seven o'clock on Christmas morning the pros,cutor was awakened by a noise downstairs. Be , got up quietly, and having half dressed himself went belOW. In the kitchen he saw the prisoner on his knees endeavour- ing to force open a bookcase with a crowbar. He seivd the man by the neck and askech "What are you doing there, you blackgnatd ?" The prisoner grasped the prosect.tor. And then struck him violently on the bead with a crowbar —a weapon about 14in. long. A furious encounter ensred, the prisoner freely using the crowbar, and the prosecutor, who is a strongly-built man. endeavouring by his strength tozet the prisoner down. Prosecutor's wife came down- stairs and went to her husband's assistance with the tongs, with which she belaboured the prisoner about the head. She was in turn struck by the prisoner, who produced from one of his pockets an old file about the length of the crow- bar, and bent at one end. The prosecutor and his wife eventually overpowered the prisoner, and the assistance of P.C. T. Jones was obtained. The parties were then taken to the Infirmary, where their injuries were attended to. Prisoner, who appeared in cour with his head bandaged completely over, has sustained etlit scalp wounds, whilst the prosecutor was also seriously ipjured about the head. Prisoner wan committed for trial at the Assizes.

TUESDAY.-13,2f)re Messrs. E. Greenall (in the chair), C. 13roadbent, W. Long, R. Pierpoint, J. Marson, and W.
C. Jones.
A•SrABBio CASE.—J.seph Dobson, a lad, 15 years of age, was charged on remand with haying unlawfully woandd William Henry Jpnes, of 27, Kontsford-road,

Warrington, at Walton enfnior, on the 15th November.— ?dr. Jenkins, who defended Dobson, also preferred a charge against Jones of having assaulted Dotison.—lt was stated in evidence that on the afternoon of Sunday, the 15th lirovenaber, Dobson and Jones, with three or four com- panions of a like age, were having a walk around by Walton Inferior. On the way they cut sticks with which they were fencing on the way. Jones having hit the stick which so n was sharpening with a knife, the latter turned oepaund and, according to his own account, said he would cut • zones across the legs if he did it again. Jones thereupon • Invited Dobson to fight, but the latter declined as it was Sunday, agreeing, however, to meet Jones on the Monday -night for the purpose of "having it out." After a few words Jones struck Dobson on the breast with his hand, and the letter retaliated by striking the comPlainant on the arm with the knife he had in his hand. Jones then struck Dobson with his stick two or three times, and the latter again struck with the knife, this time the blow being in the side. Both wounds bled, that in the side saturating • Jones' shirt with blood. After he had been struck in the side Jones fall to the ground, and Dobson then immediately threw the knife away and went to his assistance, and also helped to take him home, where he expressed his regret for what he had done. Jones was afterwards taken to the " Warrington Infirmary, where be remained about a fortnight. DC. Richmond, the house surgeon at the Infirmary, said that thd wound on Jones' arm was not of much consequence, but that in the side might have been serious. Jones' however, had completely recovered. It was stated by both Jones and Dobson that they had been friendly up to the time of the asrault, and were now again friendly. The Bench decided to reduce the charge to one of common assault, and Mr. Jesiiiins then said he would withdraw the charge of assault against Jones. and plead guittV on behalf of his client. The Chairman said the assault was a good deal owing to bad toroper. and, as he might have killed Jones, he hoped it wolVld be a warning to the defendant never again to strike in auger or with a knife in his hand. They Would impose a fine of 40e and costs, the costs being £3 18s 8.1. Pennington, Borthwick, and Haselden, three-quarter-backs; H. Varley and Twist, half-backs; Finney. Green, Rogers, Rankin, Ker- shaw, T. Vennington, and Harwood, forwards, WARRINGTON y, RUNCORN,

1 This long looked for match we played on .;aturday, iii the presence of the largest number of spectators ever seen on the Warrington football ground, fully 5,000 persons wit- nessing the game. Credit is due to Runcorn for the number they brought with them, a special train being filled, while a ,:reat number walked, and others travelled by vehicles. The keenest interest was felt as to the result of the game, which was thought would be a good trial match as to which team would have the best chance for the much coveted cup. Each team, on making its appearanc?, was loudly cheered, and the Runcorn captain, wiuning the toss of the coin, Warren kicked off, hostilities commencing in the visitors' ground. Some tight scrimmages here took place, the for- wards being evenly matched, on the ball getting loose. Some passing took place between Warren, Massey, GiPy:rt, Speakman. and Jolley, the latter being carried into touch at the Runcorn 'quarter. The next nice bit of play was a pass between Speakman, Antrobus, and Lunt, which revved play into neutral ground. Lunt next got possessioff, and kicked into touch at the home quarter. Hayes next stopped a dribble, Antrobue passing to Speakman in front of the home goal. The latter had a drop, Buxton conceding a touchdown. On starting, H. Hughes returned to Brixton, who kicked into touch. Gilbert was here teen at the head of a dribble, which Hughes stoppA by kicking into touch. Warren next invaded the visitors' 25, and here Speakman got hold of the leather, and, passing to Jolley, the latter crossed the Runcorn line, but the ball was ruled back. By some long kicking play was now taken to home quarters, where Speakman essayed another drop, the ball going dead. Soon after the leather was started again. Gilbert was con- spicuous by a dribble, Speakman intercepted a pass from Warren to Massey, end took play to the Warrington 25. J. Rigby here appeared with the ball at his toes from a scrim- mage, and took play to neutral ground, half time shortly afterwards being called. Up to this the play had been chiefly composed of scrimmages, every inch of ground being stoutly contested, the forwards being very even. on resumption of play W. Hughes set the ball rolling, play commencing in Warrington ground. The home for- wards now appeared to have the best of the packs, and quickly took the ball into the visitors' territory. Buxton improved matters by a run and kick into touch at the Runcorn 25. Scrimmages were now indulged in from which Warren neatly fed Massey, but the latter was pretty well looked after. Fair. Turner and Ashton were now seen to advan- tage, and the visitors' uprights were gradually approached. The ball was here kicked over the line, but the Runcorn full beck pluckily brought it out and kicked into touch in- side their 25. :soon after this some neat passing was put in between Warren, spealarnan, and Massey, but on the latter being charged the ball went loose and J. Rigby taking pos- session grounded it over the line, but it was ruled into play again through some rule being infringed. Speakman also crossed the line but the ball was ruled back, The ball being scrimmaged, Gilbert passed to Speakman, who made an attempt at goal, Woods touching down. On the ball being put into motion a few kicks were exchanged between the backs. it eventually landing into touch in the visitors' 25. The Runcorn forwards now made an effort, and, getting the ball loose' invaded for a minute the Warrington territory. Here the leather was kicked into the bands of Savage, who transferred it into touch in midfield. Some passing between Gilbert, Speakman; and Jolley, and dribbles by H. Ashton and Rigby, the Runcorn goal was threatened. Here the ball was kicked to Buxton, who, in grand stile rounded several of his opponents, but being pressed, kicked, the ball going dead. From the kick-out Fair. Turner returned, and War- ren following the ball up, his speed enabled him to prevent it being returned, and a scrimmage was formed in the Run- corn 25. The home forwards were now quite masters of tee game, and Fair. Turner coming with a rush grounded the ball over the Runcorn line, gaining a try near the post. The same player took the place kick but failed to improve the point. On pley being resumed, the ball travelled the field, Povey and Ashton leading the home forwards and Joule and Hughes the visitors. Warren passed to Speak- man in midfield, who took play into Runcorn ground, and a free kick brought matters dangerously near the visitors' posts. H. Hughes gave a short relief by a good dribble. but the home forwards had now all the best of the game and again visited the Runcorn goal. Rigby was here conspicu- ous with his collaring. On time being called the leather was very near the visitors, line, Warrington winning after a bard fought game by one try and two minors to two minors. In the second half the Warrington forwards had by far the best of the game, Ashton placing the ball nicely from the line-up. The Warrington hacks individually pi-eyed a good sound game. Ashton, Fair. Turner, Povey, Rigbey, and Dillon being the best of the forwards. For Runcorn, Speakman. Lunt, and Hughes were the pick of ; the backs, and W. Hughes, Joule, Broady, and Barnes, forwards.
