div.head: EXAMINER AT EDAY. JANUARY 2, 1886
div.p: THE EXAMINER AT EDAY. JANUARY 2, 1886
SHOCKING SUICIDE IN CHESHIRE.

A shocking affair occurred at Moore, near Warrington, early on Sunday morning, when a servant girl employed at the Elms. Dareebury, committed suicide by throwing her- self into the Bridgewater Canal, et a spot a few yards die- tent from the bridge spanning the canal at Moore. De- ceased was named Sarah Wittington, and was the daughter of William Wittineton, of Hightields, near Worn, Shrop- shire, a farmer. She was 22 veers of age, and was em- ployed as kitchenmaid at the 'Elms. On Saturday night she and another servant were very late at work and the housekeeper told her to leave it and go to bed. She, how- ever, appeared determined to 'finish work and refused to go, and on the housekeeper putting out the gas she re-lit it again. Snbseciaently she went out of the house, and the butler, belui..; informed of the matter by the housekeeper, made a search. Proceeding in the direction of the village he saw deceased in a crouching position at the side of the canal and called out to her. On hearing his voice she sud- denly jumped up, threw herself into the water, and was drowned. Information was given to P.C. Dutton, of the Cheshire police, who seer ch for the body, recovering it at 1-30 on Sunday morning, On the-ground at the side of the cane). SIW teVe itpronsoen which deceased had kedi ting, The body was taken to the Red Lion Jon, Moore, to await an inquest, which 7,34 t}cl4cti NOPCley efternoon by Mr. T. J. Rilgway.—The father of deceased gave evidence of ideWification. and Said he last sew his daughter alive in July, when she left home to go to the Elms. He had often heard from her, and the tone of her letters was cheerful. There were no complaints aborts her in her previous places. He knew of no reason why she should take away her life. lizabeth Bond, housekeeper at the Eime, said deceased had neen kitchenmaid there for about five months. She was vary headstrong and stubborn. On Saturday she was careless in her werk and witness spoke to her about it two or three times during the day. In the evening she told deceased to go to her supper, but she said she would not, as he was busy. Soon after eleven o'clock witness saw dr.ceaSeil in the scullery and told her that it was time to go to bed. She replied, "1 will not go to bed until I get finished." Witness turned the gae out, but on returning found that deceased had re-lighted it. Witness told her she was very disobedient, but did not speak sharply to her. She seemed very croee, laughed hysteri- cally, and went into the kitchen. Witness said, "Sarah, you are making yourself bad, go to bed," and deceased said that she would go out, and went towards the door. She said Good night, Mrs. Bond, I'll see you no more," and went out by the kitchen door. Witness went out, but could not see anything of her. Deceased seemed to kave lost her temper. She had previously given notice to leave. Wit- ness had never heard of deceased threatening to commit suicide.—Edith Burtenshaw, scullerymaid at the Elms, said that she always found deceased nice in disposition, and she .(deceased) was never in a temper with her, although they fell out a little occasionally. When they fell out deceased would be cross for a few minutes, but she would soon be all right again. On Saturday she seemed worried and not quite herself. Witness did not know why she should be worried, unless it was that she had so much work to do. She never said anything about that, except that she did not know when she was going to get through it. She had never said anything to witness about tailing her life away. On Saturday night Mrs. Bond spoke very quietly, but deceased said that it was very tantalising to her. She seemed irritated at being told to leave her work and finish. As soon as the housekeeper had put out the gas and left the room deceased lighted it again, as she wanted to finish her work that night. Witness saw her go out of the house, and she was then crying and was very excited. She said "Good night, Mrs. Bond, I'll see you no more," and went out of the house. Witness thought it was her in- tention to go through the yard and into the house again by another door. Witness could give no reason for deceased being upset, except that she had been told to go to bed.—ln answer to the jury, witness said that she did not know of deceased being in correepondence with any young man.— In answer to a gentleman representing Mr. Jones, witness said that deceased had not said when she came back from BriEhton that she wished she had thrown herself into flee sea there. She did say she hoped she would not go again, as she found the work worse.—Henry Thompson Everitt, butler at the Elms, said that on Saturday night Mrs Bond, about 11-30 o'clock, made a statement to him with respect to deceased having left the house. Witness said he knew nothing about it, but would go and look for her. He looked about the yard and then went towards the lodge and looked up the Warrington and Daresbury-roade. Witness after- wards came through the village and when on the centre of the bridge. at Moore, spanning the Bridgewater canal, he saw something laid on the towing path. He thought it was deceased, and said " Sally, come with me." She was in a crouching position. She made no answer, but suddenly got up and jumped into the water. Witness went to the spot and deceased was nearly in the middle of the water. She sank, and witness as soon as possible communicated with the police. He afterwards saw deceased taken out of the water. He had never noticed anything peculiar about de- ceased, but saw that she seemed upset on Saturday at tea time. He had always found her pleasant in every way.— The Coroner having summed up, the jury consulted in pri- trite for some time. They returned a verdict to the effect that deceased was of unsound mind when she jumped into the water..

div.head: LAND OF THE KANGAROO.
div.p: THE LAND OF THE KANGAROO.

[From the Birmingham Chronicle.] The distinguished journalist, George Augustus Sala, in a letter from Australia, published in the Louden Daily Telegraph, alludes to the fact that the Royal Mail Steam- ship (which carried him from San Francisco to Sydney), had amongst its cargo several tons of St. Jacobs Oil. As this medicinal oil has also recently been largely imported into Great Britain we were curious with regard to its efficacy. We desired Dr. Collett, M.A.., F.R.A.S., of Leitester, to test its utility, and to our surprise he has proved it to be effectual in the absolute cure of rheumatism,. neuralgia, rheumatic gout, and other cemplaints, and states that it is the most speedy and sure remedy that has come under his notice ; and if it were adopted by the general public it would prove the greatest source of happiness and comfort to many afflicted homes. So satisfied was he with its efficacy that he at once drew the attention of his brother, the Rev. J. G. Collett, of the Yorkshire Nonconformist College, Leeds, to the same; and he, knowing many needed such a remedy, at once recommended the same, and to his satisfaction found it answered in each case to which it was applied, and it has become the remedy adopted by Vie College authorities for rheumatism, as well as for sprains, bruises, Jrc., that may be received in the cricket and foot- ball fields and other places. Not only so, but Mr. George Bellbouse, of the Birmingham Fire Brigade, certifies that the members of the Fire Brigade have received great benefit from the Use of S. Jacobs Oil, in cases of severe pains in the back and knees; he also states that tender feet and other painful ailments have been immediately cured by its adoption. Yot only does he say it is good for the members of the brigade, but for their families, who praise the Oil very highly for neuralgia and kindred complaints, a few applications only being necessary to effect entire cures. .

While in London staying at a prominent hotel, we net with a gentleman (the son of a Major-General in the British Army, and who is one of the oldest baronets), who had been treated for several years by the most eminent physicians at borne and abroad, and bad been pronounced by thera in- curable, but who, by a chance conversation, was induced to apply St. Jacob's Oil. His sufferings bad been intense, and he had fer a long time been unable to wear boots. He was confined to his be for months an a time, and his limbs were strapped to a board to prevent his becoming permanently crippled. The result of the application of St. Jacob's Oil was a complete cure within a few days. This case app,,ared so remarkable that we personally investigated it, and to confirm the above statement the gentleman himself testified to the fact.

The reason we take such interest is thit we noticed in the London &win?, Times and in various medical journals, articles with reference to this remedy ; and we investigated T e cAse of a former employ* of Messrs. Davey and Moore, who are celebrated as bottle and stoneware manufacturers. This person, after tryin4 various physicians, and many medicines (some of which were supplied from St. Mary's Hospital) without effect, and being pronounced by the chief medical authorities incurable, and having suffered over six years, was admitted to the Buxton Hospital, where, after eu weeks' medical treatment, which included the use of mineral waters and baths, he obtained no relief whatever.

After trying all the remedial measures advised by friends and others, he could only move about on sticks and crutches. and experienced intense pain. By this time his joints had became greatly swollen, the sensation being as though some sharp instrument was passing through him. The physicians who attended him stated that he would be an invalid as long as he lived. A casual acquaintance in the Infirmary informed him of the remedy called St. Jacob's Oil, which be applied, and to his astonishment he found it to effect a thoroneli cure. This case has also been personally verified by the writer of this article, who has not the least interest in the promotion of St. Jacob's Oil. It is solely for the benefit of the public that we write the foregoing. and as many people need a remedy for the cure of their ailments, either contracted or hereditary, it is with confidence and sincere pleasure that we recommend this as- tooishing curative agent. FACTS WORTH KNOWING. The Bristol Times and Mirror says :—ln conversation the other day with a leading divine of Bristol, he men- tioned his experience in the use of an article in favour of which much has been said lately in several professional and other publications, the sum and substance of which being that a remedy has been found for the relief and cure of some of the most digressing ailments with which humanity is acted. The clergyman referred to, while suffering from severe lumbago, was given a bottle of this remedy by a friend, and be was delighted with the speedy cure it effected. This cruised him to recommend it to others, who hays used it with marvellous results. Our attention bay- ing been called to the matter in this way, we felt that, in the interest of our readers, it was our duty to make in- quiries on the subject among chemists and drageiste. We find that the article is universally spoken of in the highest terms. Many have expressed their feelings on paper. Mr. James Henry Gould, writes from 24, Cum- berland-street, Bristol, that he has derived so much benefit from using the preparation in question—St. Jacobs 011—that he cannot refrain from telling the wonderful benefits conferred upon him by Its use. He is an account- book maker, and suffered so severely from rheumatism, that he was compelled to relinquish his work. He consulted a doctor, and took a large quantity of medicine, but all to no purpose. An acqnaintance induced him to try St. Jacobs Oil. He used less than half a bottle, and has resumed work again, entirely free from the complaint from which he had suffered so long. We might refer before closing to the re- marka'ble case of Henry Rickette, who follows the occupa- tion of mason, and resides at Trym Cottages, Westbury, Gloucestershire. He suffered severely from rheumatism for the last two years, and early this year he was attacked so badly that he had to be cobveyed to Bath Hospital so as to have the benefit of taking the waters. His case was so serious that he was discharged in five weeks worse than when he entered. He was pronounced incurable and taken home, and then persuaded to try St. Jacobs Oil. His pain WAS so greet he could not apply it himself. His wife rubbed the oil is well, and, difficult as it may be to be- lieve, this single application entirely freed him from all pain, and he is, of course, deeply grateful for his re- covery. Mr. Ricketts also states that the remedy has been used with the same happy results in cases of toothache in his family,

div.head: RATETAYERS'-MEETING AT WIDNES.
div.p: RATETAYERS'-MEETING AT WIDNES.

THE LIBRARIES AG,T ADOPTED.—THE TOWN. HALL SCHEME SHELVED. On Tuesday M 111110; a publl6 meeting Of hitepayers was held in the Wfdnes Drill Hall to consider whether a Free Library and Public Reading Room should be under the provislAns of the Public Libraries Acts' and also whether it is desirable to at once proceed with the erection of the Tewn Hall petition of the Public Offices. Although the subjects to be disculised deeply affect the future welfare of the town, they appeared to have excited little interest amongst the ratepayers, and not more than fifty persons Put in an appearance. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., chairman of the Local Board, presided, and on the platform he was sup. ported by Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. T. Snaps, E. Carey, 'l'. Handley, D. Forster, and Boyle (assistant clerk). Amongst the audience were Dr. Hurter, Dr. McLennan, Messrs. B. Dutton, R. Webster, J. Taylor, J. Matthews, B. Brown, T. J. Peters, Showar, S. B. Stringer J. Morrison, W. Treacy, S. Sadler, T. Sadler. J. Betney, Calla.nder, M. Taylor, T. S. Swale, Atherton, H. Higginson, J. Dickson, Arc. The Chairman read the requisition calling the meeting, and thr pointed eut that the Local Board would have to keep !within an expenditure of a id in the X for the pur- poses of the Free Libraries Acts. He simply had to take the chair, he added, because he had to be the decider to a certain extent, and he should ask them not to allow him to speak to the point at all. He might state that with the , expenditure on the Town Hall the meeting had really nothing to do, and their decision on the matter could only be taken as an expression of the feelings of the rate- payers._ . _

Mr. T. Snape said the resolution which had been put into his hands was as follows I—" That the Public Libraries Acts 1855 to 1885 inclusive shall be and are hereby adopted by the Local Board for the district of Widnes." It was not his intention, he said, when he came to that meeting to take such a prominent part as be found himself doing. He had supposed that some of those who had been mere immediately interested in promoting this meeting would have moved this resolution, and he was a little astonished to find him- self in this position He, however, entertained a strong opinion in favour of the adoption of the Libraries Acts. (Hear, hear.) From his youth upwards he bad had oppor- tunities of taking advantage of. the establishment of these free libraries, or at least since the Free Libraries Act was first passed into law, ard personally he had derived such great advantage and pleasure from making use of those libraries that on that ground alone he should feel strongly in favour of extending the saute privelege to those who resided in Widnes. (Applause.) He did not known whether many of them had had an opportunity of seeing the splendid reference library they could consult in Liver- pool. Of course, these were branch lending libraries to the reference library, which was one of the finest in the King- dom. The resources of that library bad been of the greatest possible assistance to him in pursuance of study. Widnes was a town which essentially depended for prosperity and development upon the growth of knowledge and the advan- tages for the attaiement of knowledge which were held out to its ratepayers and rosidents. and he hoped they would eonsider this question not merely from a pound shilling and pence point of view. /le point-d out how gentlemen, who had extensive libraries of their ewn, found it difficult to get upon their own shelves all the things they should like and all the range of knowledge they should wish, and It therefore became necessary for them to resort to some public library upon branches of study their own shelves did not contain. They were passing through a period of great depression, and•none of them would like to see the rates increasing, though he thought from that point of view- the adoption of the Free Libraries Acts might be an economical step to take, for having succeeded in preventing the adop- tion of. more vicious practices and given recreation and amusement, and at the same time opportuni- ties for social advancerneat of the population they had thus assisted in diminishing the rates. They, also assisted in making the town a more attractive place of residence—(bear, hear,)—and those who were cot- tage owners and wished their cottages to be occupied, woula naturally wish to see a large population in the town. If they wanted a large population they must have some- thing in association with the town that would make it a more desirable place of residence. As the manufactures carried on must always detract from the residential qualifi- cations of Widnes, they ought to increase what attractions they at present possessed. He referred to the splendid library and reading-room at Northwich, given by their for- mer townsman T. Brunner, 11.P.—(applause)—and said it was a very hopeful feature in Widnes that they might look forward to haying a similar institution in their midst. He was not lea favour of a great expenditure upon this institution, and he thought the Local Board would be able to carry it on without very much expense. Any more costly schemes they had in view ought to be postpened until some more favourable occasion. He hoped there would not be a hand held no against the resolution. The library rate would be a portion of the taxes which no man he was confident would pay more cheerfully than another, for its tendency would he to stop vice, and to aseist to create an intellectual population, provide amusement and recreation which otherwise a large proportion of their fellow townsmen would not he ahle to obtain. (Applause.) Dr. O'Keeffe observed that the inhabitants of Widnes during the time the chairman had resided in it, and his honoured and respected and revered father before him, would say that he (the chairman) and his father de- served nothing but gratitude from the inhabitanta of Widnes. (Applause.) He seconded the resolution, and ar- gued that nothing would be more conducive to the moral elevation of the people of Widnes than the founding of a free library. Toere were no facilities whatever for the people of Widnes to educate themselves after they left the elementary schools, and it was after leaving those schools that working-men. and those who aspired to rise above their present positions in society, needed such facilities as a free library could afford. Deny these facilities, and a great amount of intellectual power would lie dormant and undeveloped, and would never benefit or do honour to the country. fie had been making inquiries where libraries of this kind were in use. In Helens, where the Acts bad been in force for many years, the rate to carry on the library was simply infinitesmel—not a farthing in the .£— and there was a librarian, who was paid something like £lOO a year, two assistant librarians, and ether expenses to he met. The total cost in St. Helens was something like £2OO a year. He thought a similar rate would do in Widnes. He eulogised the admirable manner in which Mr. Allen, the clerk to the Local !retard, and Mr. Handley. the chairman of the Finance Committee, bad managed the finances of the town. They had been dealt with in such an economical manner that instead of the rates being 2s 93 and 29 6d, as they were several years ago, they were now at 2s in the pound. This was a matter for which the Finance Committee and Mr. Allen deserved the highest credit. (Hear, hear.) Tho benefit that would accrue to the inhabitants of Widnes from the adoption of the Free Libraries Act would be so paramount' and the ex- pense so small, that the ratepayers would not take the latter into consideration. There was no place of entertain- ment or recreation in the town at present where the people could resort to except the publics house. Public houses were excellent institutions in their way—when they were regaired—but at the same time he must simply say that many young men, and probably many young women would prefer to spend an hour or two im- proving their minds in reading works of high class litera- ture, or even acquiring scientific attainments, such as they had in Liverpool, and possibly going in for the degrees of Oxford and Cambridge. In Widnes they had never had any gentleman or lady who had been • able to go in for the

Mr. eaandloy said if the whole scheme were carried out it was estimated that the Local Board would have to expend another £lO,OOO. They would have to repay that money within 30 years, and the interest and repay- ment of principal would amount to £578 a year. 4 penny in the pound on the present assess- ment wculd bring in £424, and to raise the required sum a rate of 13.1 would have to be laid. But it was estimated by some people that they would have a revenue from the letting of the hall. That would reduce the amount to he raised to £378. equal to a rate of jd in the X. This would mean about 7d a year on a cottage, and in preportion on other assessments. Mr. B. Brown moved that the town hall be not proceeded with at present. He thought the revenue of £2OO was very largely over estimated, and he did not think that sum was paid for rooms during the year, in Widnes. In the present condition of trade in the town he objected to increasing the permanent burdens of the town. Mr. B. Dutton seconded the motion, and asked a question. Mr. Handley replied. The present contract for the public offices was about £6,000. and it was estimated the Board would have to spend £2,500 on the Infectious Diseases Hospital. Mr. Dutton: That will increase our rates, and there will be other expenses we shall have to come to before long. The Chairman: But Mr. Dutton. we don't hope always we I shall live in a ditch. ! Dr. O'Keeffe moved an amendment that it was desirable the Board should at once proceed with the town hall por- tion of the public buildings. He said it was a shame that property cwners, large or small, should come there and be- cause they did not want to pay seven-eighths of a penny in the / prevent the other inhabitants from enjoying the bene- fits of a town hall. He appealed to their manhood and patriotism and to every manly, good, nnd generous spirit in their hearts not to be so niggardly, and not to prevent the granting of the boon of a splendid building, erected in a town which had been known all over England as the ! 'black spot on the Mersey" and which some of the people ! who lived in it have tended to promote that bad opinion about it. It was horrible and shameful. He should be ashamed to acknowledge them as his fellow citizens who had an opinion like that. (Applause.) The doctor used arguments in supporting his motion:similar to those he has brought forward at the Board meetings cad which have been reported in The Examiner. Mr. D. Forster seconded the amendmeet. contending that the town hall would be a great benefit to the town. The largest manufacturer would not pay more than £l2 a year to its cost. I Mr. Martin Taylor supported Mr. Brown's proposition. 'He stated that it was proposed to build the hall in the wrong place. It ought to be erected where the hospital was to be put up- and the hospital Isrought downwhere the waste heaps were--(The Chairman : Speak to, the point.) He had seen no valid reason why the hall should be built, ex• cope that the doctor was to be the first mayor. He did not consider that a sufficient reason why they should spend £lO,OOO. In answer to Mr. Swale, the Chairman said the totil amount stated when the plans were sent in were £15,000.— Mr. Swale: Now it is £l6,ooo.—Mr. Dutton: It will be .£2O 000.—Mr. Gould: Mr. Dutton knows. ( A laugh.) The amendment was then put, and voted for by 15 per- sons: 18 voted against ; and the original motion being put, 22 hands were held up in its favour. it was therefore de- cided not to proceed with the erection of the town hall. On the motion of Mr. Snape, secended by Mr. Carey, a vete of thanks was accorded to the chairman. Responding, Mr. Ciossage said as chairman of the meeting he bad no right to express an opinion either way, but be might now say that he thorougtily approved of the adop- tion of the Free Libraries Acts. (Applause.) Anything be could do to further the establishment of such a library and its free use he should only be too happy to do. The proceedings then closed.

As to that question there was some doubt, as there was not sufficient evi- dence to show how. they got into the lock. The only evidence was that they were seen in the street at a quarter tó nine o'clock, and thete was really no direct evidence to show how they gKinto the water. The verdict, as it seemed to him, would therefore be one of found drowned. The next question was as to whether they should make au Y presentment, Mr. Jones, representing the Bridgewater C inal Company, in answer to a question as to whether people had any legal right on the path in question, said that he dal not think that they had, but he was not able to say definitely. The Corener said that the jury could make a pre. sentiment if they wished. The company had by their silence allowed people to use the footpath, and if he belonged to the company—even although there was no legal obligation upon them to carry out the sag • g"estion of a 'pry to preserve life—he thought that he should do hi 4 best to make such provision as would prevent any loss of life. There was something be- sides a legal obligation—a moral obligation—that they had to consider. If the jury made a present- ment, he would take care that it was forwaried to the proper authorities. It was suggested by one of the jurymen that in the presentment it shotild be stated that from Fair. dough's mill as far as Half-penny Bridge should be protected. Mr. Jones said that some portion of the land did not belong to the Bridgewater Company, but they had a right of way over it. Mr. Fairclough owned to a portion of the land in that neighbourhood. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned; " and the Coroner said that he would forward present- ments both to Mx. Eairclough and the Bridgewater Canal Company. The inquiry waa then concluded.

ST. BARNABAS' NEW: SCHoOLS. OPENING CEREMONY. On Monday afternoon the handsome new day and Sun- day schools in connection with St. Barnabas' Church, War- rington, were opened by Lady Greenell. The schools present a very pleasing exterior, and inside they are cheerful and capacious. They are of a Gothic design, the elevation te Bostock-street being broken up with projections, pilasters, and penciled gables; the centre of the roof is surmounted with a bell turret, he bell being the gift of Messrs. Gibson and Son, the builders. The principal school-room is leOft. long by 28ft. wide, can be divided in the ceetre by a port- able framed partition, so constructed in sections as to form dining table tops when required, this partition when fixed , forms two schools, one for boys and one for girls. There ' are two class-rooms Mt. by 15ft., and provision is made for futuie extension, by the addition of an infants' school 251 t. Iby 201 t., blank doorways being formed for entranc to same I from the two school rooms. The entrances are from Bostock-street, and are of good width, being partly fitted ae, bat and cloak rooms with lavatories in the back portion of each. The fire places in schools and class rooms are fitted with " Shortlend " patent schoel grates, each grate having two hot-air flues, which convey warm air through two out- lets fixed in each chimney breast at about 7 feet from school floor. The cost of the buildings, including school furni- ture ef a very plain character, is about £1,200, aud has been executed by Messrs. Mit. GLADSTONE'S SEVENTY-SIXTH' BIRTHDAY. With each succeeding year the interest manifested in the anniversary of Mr. Gladstone's birth increases. Hundreds of letters and shoals of telegrams reached bins on Tuesday, his 76th birthday. The unique positioa which he at present occupies in the political world, and the fact that the eyes of men of all parties are now turned to him in an especial degree, have no doubt augmented in some slight degree the numb ,r of those who have communicated with him. But there can be no doubt that the remarkable dernotistration of public goodwill towards him which has taken place is a splendid testimonial to the value of his public services, and affords undeniable proof of the heartfelt regard eatertained for him not only in England but in every portilln of the civil- ised world. For from north and south and east and west have come messages congratulating him on having com- menced his 77th year, and expressing the ardent hope that he may for many years yet be able to serve his country. The keen chilly blast of winter has cut off many leaves from the stately trees which surround Hawarden Castle; but the cry of Mr. Gladstone's friends and admirers all over the globe—a cry expressbd in many instances in messages which flashed along the electric wire from America, New Zealand, and other distant places, as well as from numerous towns in the United Kingdom—has been that be may be spared to see many more birthdays. At the present time Mr. Gladstone is in excellent health. Notwithstanding the blinding snowstorm which prevailed in the morning, he attended divine service at the Parish Church. The remainder of the day he spent indoors. Be- lieving that there would be no chance of seeing the ex- Premier out of doors, visitors kept away. The village therefore preserved its usual quiet appearance, the only busy spot in it being the telegraph office, where the amount of work got through was greater than was ever known before. The only outward indications of the anniversary of Mr. Gladstone's birth were found in the flags which floated over the Parish Church and the lofty tower of the ancient castle. The bells of the Parish Church also rang out merry peals in the forenoon. It is absolutely impossible to give the substance of all the telegrams and letters which Mr. Gladstone received. Fore- most among them was a telegram from the Prince of Wales., who in his name and that of the Princess of Wales said : " Acceptour best wishes on the anniversary of your birthday." Other communications, some of which contained matter of a confidential and private character, were received from Mr. Gladstone's colleagues its the late Ministry, and from other leading members of both Houses of Parliament. From . Midlothian came this telegram :—" Warmest coneratula- tions frem the Liberals of Midlothian, and many happy returns of the day." Manchester sent two telegrams. One of them was couched in the following terms :—" The mem- bers of the Gladstone Club heartily congratulate you on enteriv your rith year. May many happy years till be I grauleu to yon." The following telegram was sent by the Liberals of Warrington :—" Congratulaiiens and best wishes for long continued health and happiness from the Liberals of Warrington." But other offerings of a more costly character sc,re•made to Mr. Gladstone. Early in the forenoon he received a fine bust of Achilles from Mr. S. Hazzopttlo (the Persian Cpnsul in Manchester), and Mrs Gladstone was greatly pleased with some magnificent flowers sent to her by the same gentleman. Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., gave to his father as a birth- day present a bast of the late Earl Beaconsfield. Among the other tokens of regard which were brought to the , castle was a finely tempered axe, presented to the right hon. gentleman by the Caergwrle M.anufactnring Company. So many communications reached him that it is no wonder Mr. Gladstone, with all his energy, felt himself unequal to the task of acknowledging the receipt of them. Ho there- fore requested the representatives of the press to make pub- lic the following statement, which he banded to them in M.S. :—" I have, on the recurrence of my birthday and in connection with Christmas, received many hundreds of let- ters and telegrams of congratalation and of tokens and gifts commonly showing much taste and beauty. lam deeply sensible of the kindness which is thus showered upon me from every class and quarter, often with the most touching expressions. It is only an absolute inability to deal with so extensive an addition to my large ordinary correspon- dence in a more suitable manner which makes me ask per- 'mission to convey in this public and general manner the . expression of my cordial thanks." , BANQUET AT CHESTER. The annual dinner of the Chester Liberal Club was held on Tuesday night in the Town Hall, Chester, in joint celebration of the opening of the club and of Mr. Glad- stone's birthday. Mr. W. C. Deeley, chairman of the club, presided, and amongst other guests present were Dr. Foster, M.P., Messrs. H. G. Reid, M.P, J. T. Brunner, M.P., S. Rigby, J. Beckett, John Brunner, H. M. Deeley, T. Roberts, T, W. Griffiths, and Griffiths Jones, the Revs. H. Ward Price, A. Mills, and Dr. Roberts. The customary loyal and patriotic toasts were proposed from the chair, and were heartily received by.the audience. Dr. Foster, M.P., afterwards proposed the toast "The ' Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, M.P.," and in the course of his speech said last year we drank with that love and res- pect which our great leader more than any other statesman Inspires, the health of England's Prime Minister. (Loud applause.) This year we toast the great leader of the Liberal patty, who, after carrying safely and surely the greatest change in the constitution of the country, knew how, when his Government was defeated by an " unholy alliance" On a question of the more just distribution of 1 taxatict, to retire with dignity rather than accept the posi- , tint of "a Minister on sufferance." Since then we Liberals have watched with amused attention the anxious antics of a " whole Government on sufferance—(laughter)--dreeping up its Dutch courage on illusive imaginings of a Tory reac- tion. Now that Great Britain has again exprrssad its con- fidence in Mr. Gladstone by a splendid majority, we look forward with a sure and certain hope that the new Parlia- I _ ASE—fOTRILVERT'S ruRE LARD. the a, ment will give him the power to control in a great crisis urposes. - - _ - R. THOMPSOW CO.'S SPECIAL CHRISTMAS OFFER, ISt Column of page s.—Advt. Mr. A. S. Pennington, a solicitor who had a considerable practice in Bolton, has left the town. In the Bankruptcy Court, on Wednesday, a receiving order was made against his estate.

Loss or Two LITER7OOL VFSSELS.—lntelligence has reached Liverpool of the loss of two vessels owned in that city. The ship Emily Flynn, whilst on a passage from St. John's to Fleetwood with timber, was disabled by heavy weather, and put back to the Newfoundland port. Whilst entering the harbour, however, she got upon the rocks and became a total wreck. The crew were saved. The other vessel was tke large ship Magician, which was run into and sunk by the Glasgow ship Ben Douran whilst off the Brazilian coast on a voyage from Cardiff to San Francisco. Mr. Venice, the second officer, went down with the Magician, but the rest of the crew, after three days' exposure in life- boats, reached Pernambuco. He has four j sui hte f p a . cooper (blue atone) £l4 Os sons for whom—looking at what Lord Salisbury j does for his family and what Lord Cranbrook has re-' cently done for his son-in-law—it might reasonably be supposed high places and fat incomes would be provided. But Stephen is rector of the parish in which his father lives; W. H. Gladstone has re- tired from public life, in which for a brief period he, as Lord of the Treasury, received £l,OOO a year; Herbert filled the same post for some time without taking any salary; and Henry carries on commer- cial business in far off India. Of his three daugh- ters one is married to a University Don, the third earns her own living as principal of Newnham Col- lege, and now the second one, Mary, is going to marry a curate. There is something both rare and beautiful in the contrast between the brilliancy of Mr. Gladstone's public life and the homeliness` of his private relations. In the last Parliament a profound sensation was created by the death of Mr. Wright, who, elected for Nottingham, died before he could take his seat in Parliament. The newly-elected Parliament has already had one vacancy created .in it by death, and at the present moment there are three members who are lying at death's door. The latest accounts of Mr. Forster are more hopeful, though his sickness is of a complicated character, difficult for a man of his age. to struggle against. The state of the health of Mr. Love Jones Parry before he was actually stricken down makes his case mucheworse than it otherwise might be. Active disease, when it came, found him in a condition ill calculated to resist its inroads. Mr. Talbot, member for Glamorganshire, and now H i father of the House of Commons, s sickening of the direst of all diseases, to wit, old age. He is now entering on his eighty-fifth year, and even if he gets over this present bout of illness he is not likely to be seen again in the House of Commons. These are all Liberal members, the Conservatives, with the exception of Colonel Trefusis, who died before the poll was announced, having better succeeded in meeting the toils of the contest. In addition to cases which have been made public, there are many where members, without being seriously ill, have suffered from the labours of the election. Mr. Mac- farlane, for example, who had a stormy time in travelling about his water-bound constituency, has Come home ill, with, of all things in the world. measles. Mr. Charles Russell, warned by signs of having overstrained himself, has (tone to the Riviera to recruit, and finds many members there on the same errand. . As soon as possible after the House of Commons has been constituted, its attention will be drawn to the shameless disposal by Lord Cranhrook of the office of Clerk of the Parliaments. This is a post which, if it were abolished, would not greatly affect the British constitution. A salary of £3,000 a year is attached to it. The work, such as it is, extends over only half the year, and the office is one of considerable personal and social distinction. Sir Erskine May, naturally enough, looked for the re- version of this post when it should become vaeant. Ile has for more than a generation rendered con- spicuous service in the House of Commons at a lower salary than that paid for the ornamental office in the House of Lords. There is not the slightest doubt that had the Liberal Government been in power when Sir William Rose died, Sir Erskine May would have obtained the pro • motion But it falling out otherwise, Lord Cranbrook has clutched at the appointment, and positively be- stowed it upon his son-in-law. The thing is in itself incredible, but it is officially an- nounced in the "Gazette." If Lord Cranbrook were a poor man. and could not afford to endow his daughter, some kind of excuse might be made. But he is one of the wealthiest peers, and might well feel ashamed thus to deal with public monies. What makes the thing worse is that the other natural candidate passed over is Mr. Disraeli. To Mr. Disraeli's brother Lord Cranbrook owes his T)olitical advancement and his peerage. The late Mr. Disraeli took him u p when he was a plain eoun-

"THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND IS IN DANGER." Sir,—You will be kind enough to accept the above asser- tion as a fact. The Bishop of Liverpool is my authority for the statement, or I should scarcely have ventured it. Accepting his Lordship as an authority on Church matters, it may not be amies to examine, in as humble a manner as possible, his reasons for so alarming a statement. I should say, first. that I quite accept and agree with the statement that "the Church is in danger," yet I go a little further than the good Bishop as to the cause. The Bishop gives eight reasons for this danger.

First, we have the" undying enmity of the Church of Rome." Many of your readers will be. somewhat astonished at the prominence given to this reason. In Warrington we have recently witnessed a pillar of the Protestant Church paving humble deference to the representatives of the Church of Rome, contributing largely to new altars, and having the satisfaction of hearing the priest advise that in return for such munificient kindness, they; must do their best to place the kind gentleman at the head ef the poll. What matters it to either priest or parson that the recipi- ent of all this kindness is one whose chief aim and object in life is to disfigure street corners with tempting palaces, whereby workmen's earnings may be filtered through, and sweetly jingle into the pockets of parson, priest, and pub. lican. The Churches work with the publican and brewer in hope of dividing the spoil. Bishop Ryle makes a mistake in describing the enmity that exists between the rival Churches as being " undying:" As a matter of fact it is love, unquenchable love, that im- pels the Church of Rome forward in her desire to absorb all that the English Church is so anxious todefend—love,of cash, " sweet cash." Bishop Ryle forgets that there is so much In common between the two Churches. Cardinal Manning, in a pastoral recently issued, says:—" The Roman Catholic Church is toiling with all its might against the attempt to make education, from the Board schools to the Universities, secular and lay." Pope Leo XIII., writing to the Cardinal with reference to the education of the people, commends this attitude, and speaks of this island of ours as the " mother of saints," and is kind enough to tells that he "loves us with a paternal charity." Here we have the Church of Rome and the Established Church of England in entire sympathy with each other, upon the most important of all questions, education. I have no intentien of dealing seriatum with the eight reasons put forward by the Bishop of Liverpool. I much prefer to read the signs of the times, and they most dis- tinctly point out that the Bishop is right in his conclusions; "the Church is in danger," and why? The answer to this question might be given in one word, be- cause it is founded on falsehood. I much prefer to give as a reason, because it has not won the hearts of the people. Has it not been the boast of the Church that she placed in every village a cultivated gentle- man ? Has it not been her boast that hers was the educa- ting influence to which Englishmen owed so much? The English farm labourer is not ungrateful. The slightest token of sympathy from the parson or the squire would have been repaid threefold. The elections just over have exposed to the world bow fragile has been the bond of sympathy and how soon it has snapped, and now the par- son turns round and publicly states that "in intelligence the farm labourer is no better than a pig." If this be so, who is to blame? Is Bishop Ryle willing to admit with the Bishop of Chichester," That the agricultural labourer , resents, and justly, his virtual degradation in the Church I which is his own " ? - _

Lord Macaul,4y, in one of his essays, tells us that "The Church uf England has continued for more than 150 pears to be the steady enemy of public liberty." Not a doubt can remain as to the conduct of the Church in the past. Seek- ing its own aggranciflement, it has made friends of the mammon of unrightzousness, and now it cries out for reform _ . -

We judge of the Chnrch by its fruits. In the country districts it has been all powerful. In the towns, especially the large towns, its influence has for years been nil. In the towns the cheap paper competes with the school in educating the masses. The result may be summed in the words of Countess Cowper, who, in an article in "The 10th Century" says, speaking of the east end of. London ;—" I should say there was far less drankenness and immorality there, in proportion to numbrs, than there is in the differ- ent county parishes I have to do with." Bishop Ryle will do well to ponder a little and grasp the meaning of these words to their full extent; immorality and drunkenness abound in districts where the Church has reigned supreme. I have no doubt the Bishop has received a circular marked " private and confidential " from Mr. W. Allison, editor of the Conservative News Agency, Limited. In this circular all good Conservatives are asked to take shares and influence others to do so. I suppose the " others "alluded to would be Liberal Churchmen, and what do you think, sir, is to be done with the money so subscribed? Why, nothing less than to print and distribute "leaflets and cartoons." Unless this is done the "English Church is doomed." The Church is going to reform herself by distributing cartoons amongst the agricultural labourers, whom the parsons tell us are on the same level in intelligence as pigs.

div.p: M A RKETS.
THE PENWORTIIOI BRIDGE DISPUTE.

The adjourned annual session of County Justices was held at Preston on Thursday. Estimates of the probable expenditure on county administration to the end of August next were submitted, and the necessary levies of rates were authorised. Several memorials were presented against the proposed construction of a bridge ever the river Ribble, between Pres- ton and Peuwortham Brow, at the cost of the ratepayers of the county. The principal memorial was that presented by Mr. J. Ry.lands, from the Poor Law Guardians of Warring- ton Union, in which complaint was made on behalf. of the ratepayers of the special hardship and wrongs which would be done to them if they were rated for the new bridge from which they could never derive the least advantage. The me- morialists state that when a new bridge was built at Caton, on the Lune, all the costs were equitably charged on the Lone- dale hundred and on the town of Lancaster, and they were , unable to reconcile one proceeding with the other. A hun- dred years ago the county justices declined to make the county liable ler a similar bridge yet, as it might to some extent be useful to the county, they contributed £2.000 to- wards its erection on condition that the county be thence- forth free from liability. The proposed improvement, the memorialists stated, would materially improve the value of, land in Penwortham, and otherwise afford many advantages to the people residing there, yet the persons so benefited would contribute very trifling sums to the great cost of the improvement, and to the Parliamentary and other expenses, which in their first stage amcunted to £5,000. Mr. W. H. Higgin, Q.C., as chairman of the Parliamen- tary Bridge.,Qprnmittee, moved, "That the bill now before the court authorising the construction of an approach road to the bridge authorised by the Penwortham Bridge Act, 1885, and of a short railway or tramway between the luna- tic asylum at Whittingham and the railway station at Grim- eargb, and for other purposes, be approved, and that the Penworthain Bridge Committae be requested to superintend and promote the progress of the said bill through Parlia- ment." He explained that this resolution had been forced upon the committee by Parliament; it was net through any wish of their own that it was brought forward ; and be urged that if the court adopted the prayer of the memo- rialists it would act in direct opposition to everything they had hitherto done. The committee had been in negotiation with the Corporation of Preston and with the Leyland Hun- dred Highway Board, and they were just on the point of arriving at a satisfactory conclusion. They met en the previous day, and everything seemed to be favourable for a settlement of matters between them. Mr. Fell seconded the motion.
Mr. Assheton said he could not see!his Way to accept the proposition of the committee with respect to Penwor- tham Bridge. _ _ _

Mr. Hibbert suggested that the court should not approve clause 10 in the bill, which threw the expense of making the road on the county bridge rate. It should be thrown on the Leyland hundred bridge rate. It was found, how- ever, that this was not practicable. Mr. Townsend said that when this matter was last before the court, many magistrates voted for the bill, net knowing that Preston did not contribute anything at all to the county bridges. Mr. John Rylands proposed as an amendment •4 That no further proceedings be taken f relating to Penwortham Bridge until the court shall so determine."

Mr. Bleckley seconded the amendment,and said he objected to the committee going again to Parliament. It would be bezinning afresh, and they had already spent £5,000. It was like throwing money away lavishly. He strongly pro- tested against gentlemen coming to that court and voting in hvour of proceedines to benefit their own property. Sir, Richard Cross's name had been mentioned as a member of the committee ; lett be had promised to do all he could to have the rating clauses altered. Mr. Thovstorne said Mr. Bleckly had come there to show that this was a matter of Personal benefit to him if the bridge were built. Wall, he did net deny it. It would ha a great benefit to him and his property. It would bring his laud 800 yards nearer to Preston. But the question was, not whether it would benefit him, but whether it was a !egitimate improvement to make at the hands of the county. He said it would be, because the present bridge was unsafe.
After some further discussion, Mr. Rvlands' amendment was carried by 65 votes to 42, and was then agreed to as a substantive motion.

LA_ l' NEWS.
The wife of Mr. George Augustus Sala has died .at Mel- bourne. Mr. Svdn•y Button bss consented to join the Royal Commission on Education.

The annual distribution of her Majesty's New Year's gifts, amounting to £220, and consisting of meat and coals, was made on Friday to the Windsor poor. A telegram despatched from Torquay at six o'clock last evening states that Mr. Forster has passed a quiet day, and tnat there is no new feature to report. Messrs. Briscoe and Sons have secured the contract for 40,000 tons of steel rails and 40 000 tons of fittings for use on the Victoria Government Railway. On Thursday night the steamer Blonde, outward bound for Dunkirk, came into collision with the Tiber, and sank abreast of Tilbury Causeway. The crew were saved and taken to Gravesand. THE WELSH STRIKE.—Mr. Assheton Smith on Friday re- fused the proposal of the workmen to rafer to arbitration the dispute at the Llanberis slate quarries. The men moved a resolution to continue the strike.

PAPAL GENEROSITC—The Pope, in addition to other very large Christmas alms, has converted all the presents made to him personally for some years past into money, and given the proceeds, amounting to half a million francs, to the Pro- paganda. THE EMPEROR WILLIAM'S JUBILEE.—Lord Wolseley left Charing Cross terminus on Friday morning for Berlin; to represent the Queen at the celebration on Sunday of the 25th anniversary of the Emperor William's accession to the Prussian throne.

_ Ax AGED COUPLE DROWNED. —As William Brown, rivet maker, Greenock, and his wife, who had been at the marriage of their granddaughter, were walking home on Friday morning in the darkne-s along the east side of the Victoria harbour, they fell into the river and were drowned. Both were over 60 years of age. THE PATENTS ACT.—The President of the Board of Trade has arvointed Sir Ferrer Herschel!, the Earl of Craw- ford and Balcarres, and Baron Henry de Worms, M.P., to be a committee to inquire into the duties, organ:Elation, and arranitements of the Patents Office under the Patents, Designs, and Trade Marks Act, 1883. .

DISTRESS IN IRELAND.—The Central News learns that the unprecedented distress which prevails among the poor peasantry in the North-West of Ireland, more particularly at Ache!, Innishoffin, and Eagle islands, has caused the Cable News• Company of New York to open a subscription for the benefit of the sufferers. The Brooklyn Young Irish- man's National League have sent a special contribution t,) the relief fund.
ANOTHER LOVER DROWNED —On Thursday evening an

inquest was held at Uppertnill, Saddleworth, on the body of Esther Buckley Schofield; 21, who was drowned on Sunday night. She was returning home with her lover by the canal side at Uppermill, when he fell into the lock. She ran for assistance, and, stumbling in the darkness, fell into the water. He was rescued, but her dead body was found the morning afterwards. A verdict of " Accidentally drowned" was returned.

THE DEEPENING OF THE DEE.—The costly and diffi- cult work of deepening the navigable channel of the Dee is being pushed forward as rapidly as possible under the su- perintendence of Mr. Leader Williams, 8.C., and Mr. Hy. Taylor, C.E , Chester. Already a manifest improvement has been efected, and vessels drawing eleven feet of water are daily towed up and down on a moderate tide, which before would inevitably have grounded. Only a short time ago a vessel lay aground over a fortnight. AN INDIGNANT IRISH LANDLORD.—A "Landlord,' in the Dublin Express, says the country never was in so bad a state. The League of Hell never before was so organised. Having refused to reduce judicial rents. he has had to serve 73 ejectmenta by post, process-servers decliniag through fear. On a neighbouring property, the police are guarding a process-server two days in their barracks, which is be- sieged by hundreds, and tenantry, and even the police, cannot stir out; while the popelace are marching four deep and drilling in the street. The landlord had asked the priest lc make a settlement. The writer does not indicite the part of the country.

div.head: MAJOR TROTTER'S VISIT TO EGYPT.
div.p: MAJOR TROTTER'S VISIT TO EGYPT.

CONST-A7N-T-I-NOPLE, Turrasnes.—The departure for Egypt of Major Trotter, the military attache to the British Em- bassy here, has no connection with Sir H. D. Wolff's mis- sion. Sir William White communicated with Lord Salis- bury Major Trotter's wish to proceed to E4ypt on Nay. of absence in.-order to accept a long standing invitation of a friend. fiord Salisbury in reply telegraphed that Sir Wil- liam White might grant Major 'Crofter one month's leave if he did not require his services.

SPANISH TREATIES. MADRID, FRIDAY.—The Cortes will, probably accede to the Government propoeal to prolong until 1852 the com- mercial treaties about to expire. THE PRENCH MINISTERIAL CRISIS. Pants, FRIDAY MORNING.—LittIe progress has been made towards forming a CAbinet. The crisis is likely to be pro- longed for several days. It is thought in any case that M. Ciemenceau will be prevailed upon to take the Ministry of the Interior.

ENGLAND AND BURMAti. RANGOON, FRIDAY, 7 A.st.—A grand parade of the troops of the garrison has just been held, at which, in the presence of a large concourse of natives, a proclamation, issued hY the Earl of Pufferin in the name of the Queen-Empress, was read, notifying the annexation of Upper Burmah to the British Empire.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

LYBENZ G 11113151111 Sca-o-o-L.2--T- he terminal examination has just been concluded. The qead master, Mr. W. Heslop, M.A., is able to report very satisfactory progress throughout the school, and has the greatest pleasure in testifying to the general good conduct and admirable tone displayed by the pupils. The examination showed that the following boys were at the head of their respective forms :—Third form, Wheeler; second form, Sandbach ; first form, Cle -g. We understand that two scholarships for boarders (open to boys b.tween the ages of 10 and 13) will be awarded o^ or about the 16th of January.

div.head: NEW YEAR AT LYMM.
div.p: NEW YEAR AT LYMM.

There were very few special observances of New Year at Lvmm, and yesterday business was not geaerally suspended. On Thursday night and early on New Year's morning the church bells were rung, and two bands playel in various parts of the village. A watch-night service, commencing at eleven o'clock, was held in the Wesleyan Chapel, wnen Messrs. Boyd, Ashton, Mort, and Young gave short ad- dresses.

CAROL sntoEns.—A band of carol singers, organised by Mr. H. J. Duman, connected with the Earlestown Gospel Mission, met on Chris?mas Eve at the Co-operative Hall, and, accompanied by the string band, afterwards visited the residences of friends and supporters of the Mission, where they sang seasonable anthems. A party of 20 memlprs of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars, under the conductorship of Mr. George Clarke, sang Christmas carols at various places. and concluded by partaking of an enjoyable "supper" at the Welcome Coffee Palace. The Wargrave Church choir, and the Vul- can Wesleyan choir, also sang at various places. NEWTON CRICKET AND BOWLING CLI7R.—In aid of the funds of the Newton Cricket and Bowling Club a miscel- laneous concert was held in the Town Hall, Newton. on Tuesday evening. Though the weather was very unfav• ourable there was a large and enthusiastic audience, who manifested their hearty appreciation of the entertainment by repeated applause. Mr. T W. Stanfield's selections on the violin were finely executed ; and the humourous pieces by Mr. Lester Barrett, of Manchester, occasioned consider- able amusement. Mr. C. H. Havt-es nicely sung "The wandering minstrel " and " The stirrup cup," and Miss Haynes appeared to advantage in "'The click of the ,wicket " and "Within a mile of Edinburgh town." DuetF , by Messrs. J. and W. Parker (concertina and whistle res- , nectively) were highly attractive, and Captain Hugh F. Goocla (of the Vulcan) was deservedly encored for his rendering of .‘ Who krows and "The soldier's farewell." rho popular artiste, Mr. George Barton, of St. Helens, was encored on each appearance, and Miss Gorse was well re' uived in her interpretations of "The minstrel hoc " and 'The storm." Miss Scrymgeour sang " Sissie" and "The better land," and duets were given by Mr. C. H. and Miss Haynes and Miss Gorse and Mr. Barton. Mr. P. Fairclough was the accompanist.

. WARRINGTON. ST. PAL-L.B CHuncu.—There was a large congre- gation at the evening service at St. Paul's Church on Sunday, when a sermon in aid a the Curate Fund, was preached by the Rev. Canon Dodd, -vicar of Stretton. After the blessing had been pronounced, carols were sung, the recessional hymn, "Through the night of doubt and sorrow," bringing the service to a elose.

"Miss ANGELA FENTON."—This lady—who, it is well known, is the wife of Colonel. Greenall— with her London company, is advertised to appear in the Public Ilail,Warrington, on the 15th and 16th January, and it may safely be augured that her visit will be of interest to a much wider circle than that of the ordinary playgoers of the town and neigh- bourhood. On the occasion of her visit here Miss Fenton will represent the part of " Gilberte " in the comedy of " Frou Frou,' and also that of the heroine in a new comedy. The proceeds of the first evening's performance will be given to local charities.

SUDDEN DEATH—On Tuesday afternoon John Knockton, labourer (40), who resided at Pye's-yard, Old-road, Latchford, died rather suddenly. He was engaged in carrying bars. weighing about lcwt. each, from waggons at Dallam Forge to a pile about 20 yards distance, when he was seen by a man named John Taylor to be on the ground as though ill. Taylor got out of the waggon, and seeing that deceased was helpless, at once went for medical as- sistance. Deceased was taken into some adjoining stores. On the arrival of Dr. Fox that gentleman pronounced that the poor fellow was dead. Mr. Blunt, deputy coroner, held an inquiry relative to the occurrence at the Norton Arms on Thursday morning, when a verdict of death from natural causes was returned.

TEA PARTY AT WARRINGTON.—On Monday even- ing the members of the second-class (males) belong- ing to Wycliffe Sunday School held their annual tea party in the lower vestry. An excellent tea was provided, of which nearly 50 persons, both male and female, partook. A varied programme of in- strumental and vocal music was after-Wards crone through, the following ladies and gentlemen officiat- ing :—The Misses Pickavance, E. Brown, Rathbone, Podmore, and Ball; and Messrs. E. Pickavance, sen., teacher of the class; S. Jeffrey, and J. Pod- more, the last named gentleman acting as accom- panist. During an interval in the programme, the Rev. J. Yonge and Mr. Pickavance delivered short addresses, and a vote of thanks to those who had taken part in the entertainment and had assisted in preparing tea was carried with.acclama- tion. , ODDFELLOW'S FUINIERAL.-011 Sunda/ t-he ns of Brother Samuel Crocker were interred in the Warrington Cemetery. Mr. Crocker was a member of the Olive Branch Lodge (NO. 1,380) of the, Inde- pendent Order of Oddfellows -(Manchester 'Unity), and had been treasurer for the last seven years, and lodge 'book examiner for the past two years, The deceased was 36 years of age. Amongst the brethren present were the following :—George Perry, Prey. G.M. ; John Emson, Prov. C.S. ; P.P.G..11.'s Dom.ville, James Beswick, James Leyland, Matthew Knowles, and J. H. Norbtiry, and P.G.'s Thomas Kenyon, T. C. Brookes, ThOmas Wadsworth, James Dagnall, Gil- bert Riley, John Riley, J. Winstanley, H. Dutton, Baines, P. Warburton, Thomas Lilley, Thos. Thros- sell, William Throssell, F. Taylor, W. Dainteth, J. Littlewood, W. Haigh, ,Thomas Wright, E. Jennings, T. Bradshaw, J. Buckley, and Lowden Wells, under- taker. The following relatives were also present : Messrs. Joseph Crocker, J. and L Astley, W. Craw- ford, and George Mounfield. . THE BRITISH WORKMAN PUBLIC-HOUSE CO., LIMITED.—It is encouraging to note that, at a time when small profits and scanty dividends are so often complained about; the above Company is still carrying on its- admirable work successfully and profitably. At the annual general meeting of shareholders which was held last week in the Com- mittee Room of the Horsema.let-street House, a prosperous balance sheet was presented, and a . dividend of 10 per cent. declared. Mr. T. Morris presided at the meeting, and there were also pre-. sent Alderman Holmes; Mr. W. Long, Dr. GornalL and others. The airman congratulated the share- holders upon the continued success of the company, and, referring • to- the number of houses belong- ing to private individuals in the same way, , of business, which had been opened since-the corm pany commenced its operations, said he. had no feeling of jealousy towards them, but rather re- joiced that they, along with them, were helping to, provide attractions forthe working man in addition to those to be found in the ordinary public house. The retiring directors, Messrs. Noah Legge, J. If. Gornall, J. Garner, William Long, and Peter Clare, were re-elected, as were also the two auditors, Messrs. George J. Brown and J. W. Bouchier. Thanks were awarded to the Chairman, the Cora- mittee, the Sec. (Mr. 11. Roberts),and the other officers of the company, It may be-mentioned- that, for the. purpose of facilitating the relief of the unemployed people of the town, the company have intimated. that persons desiring to relieve the distressed. by providing food, instead' of giving money, may pur- chase tickets at the rate of 13 for is.. and each of these tickets will enable the recipient to obtain, food to the value of Id'.. at any of the company 'S I houses. A COLLISION ON THE ROAD.—At Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, William Gleave, farmer, of Burtonwood, sued Thomas Higgins, blacksmith,. Legh-street, Earlestown, to recover the sum of 1:2611s, fordara- aoes to a mare, and loss sustained by- him, through the negligence of the defendant in driving a horse and' trap on the New-road, Earlestown, on the 15th August last.—Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr: H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. Helens, was for the defendant. —Mr. Davies, in an opening' statement to his Honour, said ' that the claim was made up as follows :—Damages, £5 ; ten week's keep of the mare during the time th at she was unfit to work, at 7s per week,,E3 lOs ;doss of services of the mare, at 6s per day, £ls;' veter- inary surgeon's account, £2 is 6d;- and Mr Thomas Pope's (farrier) account, 19s 6d ; total, £26, Hs. On the 15th of August last, Mr; Davies. said, the plaintiff's man., who was also his uncle; was taking milk from plaintiff's farm. to a Mr. Jones, at Earlestown. 'A mile away from the farm, at Burtonwood, he overtook Mr. William George and Charles Shaw, who got into the- • cart. They drove a considerable distance towards Earlestown, and when about 100 yards down the New-road at Earlestown the defendant Higgins drove *past them at a sharp pace with a pony. When he had got about 40 yards ahead, be drew up on his. wrong side of the road and allowed plaintiff's vehicle to pass him. When they had gone a distance past him, defendant came us again at a furious pace, and when level' with plaintiff's trap. deliberately drove into it, inflicting the damages for which claim was now made. The defence was that the damage sustained by plaintiff did not amount to more than £1 or Li 10s., and also that the plain- tiff's cart was on the wrong side of the road. The case was not concluded when the court rose and the hearing was therefore adjourned. FREEMASONRY IN WARRINGTON.—The Festival of St. John, bodge of Lights, 148, was ce.brated on Monday, when Brother Edward Greenall, jun., the W.M. elect, was duly installed according to ancient custom. The ceremony was conducted by Brother W. 11. Robinson, P.M., 148. After the installation the W.M. appointed the following officers for the ensuing year, and invested them with the insignia of their offices, viz.:—Brothers T. Mee Pattison, I.P.M. and organist; Thomas. Robinson, S.W.; John Hesketh, J.W. • W. Percy, S.D, ; Walter IL Young, J.D. ; W'. R. Hill, I.G. ; Thos. Grime, P.M., treasurer; and W. H. Robinson, P. 11., secretary. After the investiture of the officers, the W.M. presented Brother Pattison with a past master's jewel in com- plimentary terms. Brother Pattison having thanked the members for their kindness, the lodge was closed. in the usual manner. An adjournment was then made to the Patten Arms Hotel, where a rechereki banquet was provided, to which nearly forty sat down. The W.M. (-Brother Edward Green- all, jun.) proposed the usual loyal toasts, which were duly honoured. Brother Hindley, P.M. then gave "The Right Hon. Earl Lathom, Prov.G.M., and the P.G. officers," coupling with the toast the names of Brothers Tunstall and Finney, who responded. Brother Thomas Sutton proposed :" The W.M. and brethren of 1,250," and Brothers.: W. Bolton, WM., and W. H. Jenkins, I.P.M. of 1,250, acknowledged the compliment. Brother T. M. Pat- tison then proposed the health of the W.M. in com- plimentary terms, which the Worshipful Master acknowledged. Brother Dr. Mackie next gave "The past masters and- officers of lodge 148," Bro- ther Pattison, 1.P.M., responding. Brother Dr. H. Young gave "The -visitors," to which Brother Cap- tain Webster, whose health was conjoined, replied in an appropriate speech. The toast of "The musi- cal brethren," "The charities," and "The installing Master haying been given and heartily receited, the Tyler's toast brought the Festival of St. John to a successful termination. The musical portion of the programme was carried out in a first-class man- ner by Brothers T. M. Pattison, J. T. Jones, Q. F. I Curzon, W. H. Jenkins, and, Walter Young.

There is a feature in this circular that may be interesting to Canon Dodd. It is distinctly an appeal to the Conserva- tive party, yet the Canon tells us that " the Church must have no party." I shall be interested in knowing what amount the Canon subscribes to Mr. Allison's " Conserva- tive News Agency " for the scattering of "cartoons " over the country." Bishop Ryle may take my word for it, that the words John Bright recently uttered will find an echo in every honest man's heart, via :—" Is it not strange that priests aad parsons of Rome, and of her sister the Established Church, should always be found in partnership with political dark- nese and evil."
